en: Dharma Master Yuan compiled and arranged [this work] to clarify the number of births undergone by *srotāpannas*. Within it, there are four distinct sections of analysis:
first, clarifying the number of bodies received by *srotāpannas*; second, clarifying the number of grades of delusions moistened; third, clarifying...
Regarding the extent to which afflictions moisten rebirth,
the fourth [section] clarifies the extent to which the severing of delusions diminishes rebirth.
First, concerning the number of bodies received in rebirth:
There are four types of *srotāpanna*.
The first person, having practiced with diligence in the present life, attains the fruit of *arhatship*;
thus, they enter *parinirvāṇa* in that very same body.
As for the second person, who currently practices and attains the fruit of anāgāmin, they will receive a body in the higher realms;
they may experience one more birth, or two, three, four, or even as many as the maximum possible.
Alternatively, one may receive fifteen or sixteen [precepts].
Regarding the "fifteen":
for a person who attains the meditative absorption of bliss, there are four dhyānas, and throughout their births, there are eleven bodies.
The first dhyāna has two locations;
each of the three higher dhyāna stages has three locations.
Together, these constitute eleven.
By adding the four spheres of emptiness, there are fifteen.
As for the statement "sixteen," there is a person of joyful wisdom who produces eleven bodies throughout the four dhyānas.
Including the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*), there are sixteen.
These distinctions are explained in detail later.
As for the third type of person, having manifested in this body, they attain the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and receive a body within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Among humans and devas, they will undergo either two births or one birth.
As for the fourth person, in this present life they realize only the first fruit (srotāpatti) while still receiving a body within the desire realm.
They may undergo one birth, or two, three, four, or even up to a maximum;
they undergo seven births, or fourteen births through coming and going.
Having died from these fourteen, they undergo them by coming and going among humans and devas.
One must not treat them as equivalent. Why is this so?
Because it is due to the mind that perceives suffering and feels weary detachment.
This stream-enterer (srotāpanna), having previously contemplated suffering and experienced an abundance of mental afflictions regarding suffering,
when taking birth among humans, perceives human suffering and seeks birth in the heavens;
when taking birth in the heavens, he again perceives the faults of the heavens and seeks birth among humans.
Therefore, they do not arise simultaneously. Question:
Among those fourteen births, in which one does birth occur first?
This meaning is not fixed.
One may attain the Way among humans, then, having relinquished the human body, first dwell among the devas;
or one may attain the Way among the devas, then, having relinquished the deva body, first be born among humans.
Therefore, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* states:
"Among humans, one transcends the human realm for seven full lifetimes;
it is the same among the devas."
Question: Why is it that there are exactly seven returns, neither more nor less? Answer:
Because they are sustained by the power of karma, they do not fall short of seven returns.
Because they are restrained by the power of the Path, they do not exceed seven returns. Furthermore,
the force of karmic power reaches its limit at this point,
just as with the seven medicinal trees, the seven-step venomous snake, the seven-day medicine, and the seven types of worldly affairs.

Question: Regarding this person who, after having passed through seven returns, attains only nirvana— there are differing views in the sūtras and śāstras concerning those who are born into higher realms.
According to the Abhidharma and the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
all noble ones who have previously been born within the stages of the desire realm,
having developed a profound sense of revulsion toward suffering, do not at all take birth in the higher realms.
Regarding the attainment of nirvana within a body belonging to the desire realm,
according to what is taught in the *Aśokarājāvadāna-sūtra*, there are those who are reborn in higher realms; that sūtra proclaims:
There is a sutra concerning the sick Srotāpanna Upacūḍa, who manifested five pure bodies through transformation.
It clarifies that he attained rebirth in the heavens;
the causes and conditions of this transformation are fully detailed as explained in the sutra.
There are four stages in the classification of *srotāpanna*.
Among these four types of persons, the first is called the *srotāpanna* who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*).
The middle two are called the *srotāpanna* who progresses in the present life (*abhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*).
The last one is called the *srotāpanna* who takes birth;
next, the second section clarifies the number of categories of defilements that moisten rebirth (*upapatti-sneha*) for a *srotāpanna* taking birth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The afflictions that produce rebirth are divided into three coarse categories,
nine subtle categories,
and five intermediate categories.
The three coarse divisions are:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
This meaning is not fixed.
Discussing it in terms of faults, those coarse afflictions with heavy faults are described as superior,
while those subtle afflictions with minute faults are described as inferior.
That which is neither coarse nor subtle is called "middling.
If judged by its power and effort, that which is coarse, superficial,
and possesses weak power to obstruct the Path is designated as "inferior."
Subtle afflictions have deep roots;
because their power to obstruct the Path is strong, they are described as "superior.
Intermediate afflictions differ from the former and are therefore called "intermediate."
Therefore, the Sūtra ought to state that the power of the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*) is supreme.
For now, we shall provisionally divide [the categories] according to the first sense.
Gross afflictions are designated as superior;
subtle ones are called inferior;
those between the two are described as middling.
As for the ninefold subdivision, there are three grades within each of the coarse and intermediate levels,
namely: the highest-of-the-high, the middle-of-the-high, and the lowest-of-the-high.
The intermediate delusions are also threefold:
namely, intermediate-superior, intermediate-middle, and intermediate-inferior.
The subtle delusions are also threefold.
What are called the lower-upper, the middle-lower, and the lower-lower;
and the fivefold division of the middle:
namely, the lower-middle, the upper-middle, the upper-upper, the uppermost, and the middle [of the upper].
The first two are called "superior-superior";
the next two are "superior-middle";
and the next two are called "superior."
The next two are called "middling," and the last one is called "inferior.
These five correspond to the five stages of the *vāsanā-dhyāna* (perfuming meditation); their meanings are similar when their respective stages are distinguished.
Question: Dividing [the moisture] into nine categories is sufficient; why trouble oneself by explaining five? Answer:
Now, for the purpose of clarifying the degree of moisture based on this, it is necessary to distinguish them.
Next, the third section clarifies the extent to which the afflictions (*kleśa*) moisten rebirth.
Within this, there are three sub-sections of analysis.
The first clarifies which afflictions possess the capacity to moisten and which do not.
Second, it clarifies the differences in how afflictions moisten rebirth;
third, it clarifies the extent to which various afflictions moisten rebirth.
Regarding the first point, concerning which afflictions moisten and which do not:
Some assert that among the nine grades of afflictions, those not severed by the vehicle cannot moisten rebirth,
whereas those severed by the vehicle are used to moisten rebirth.
This interpretation is incorrect.
Once the vehicle has been severed, it can no longer moisten rebirth;
yet when it was not yet severed, why did it not moisten?
You should know this.
All [karmas] are equally able to moisten birth;
however, there are two types of moistening:
first, that which directly moistens the arising of birth through its present manifestation.
Second, there is the accomplishment of latent assistance and nourishment.
For one whose vehicle has been severed, even before it is fully severed, there is the principle of latent assistance and nourishment;
there is also the principle of manifest, direct nourishment.
How can it be that [the seed] exists?
The meaning is as explained later. This concludes the first section.
Next, we clarify the different ways in which afflictions (*kleśa*) moisten rebirth.

Among those nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which ones arise manifestly to directly moisten rebirth, and which ones are possessed as latent dispositions to provide the nourishment for rebirth?
To discuss these in order: among all the afflictions, the most superior and coarse grade arises manifestly with respect to its object to directly moisten rebirth.
The remainder are all accomplished through the moisture of the provisions for rebirth.
According to the actual reality, the arising of delusions has no fixed order;
the examples of the initiation of karma and the moistening of rebirth are not uniform.
The degrees of delusion—superior, middling, and inferior—are not fixed.
What is the meaning of this?
At the time of taking birth, there may be a person of dull faculties.
If one perceives a superior condition that gives rise to a predominant fetter (*adhimātra-saṃyojana*),
then this fetter itself directly moistens the process of rebirth,
while the middling and inferior [fetters] provide assistance.
There are those of middling faculties who,
encountering middling conditions, give rise to middling fetters;
they then use these very fetters to directly moisten and sustain rebirth.
The afflictions of the upper and lower realms are established and provide mutual assistance.
There may be those with sharp faculties who,
encountering weak conditions, give rise to afflictions of the lowest grade.
Thus, by means of this, one forms bonds, experiences moisture, and undergoes rebirth;
the superior and middling [karmas] provide assistance accordingly. Regarding those who undergo rebirth through the superior [karma], they will certainly receive many bodies.
The intermediate fetters are fewer than those,
and the lower fetters are the fewest of all;
thus, although the nine grades of afflictions of a srotāpanna have not yet been entirely severed, this does not prevent the number of rebirths from being indefinite.

For this reason, among the nine grades of afflictions, those that are to be abandoned by subsequent cultivation may also arise in the present; having thus completed the assistance for moistening karma and taking rebirth, these two sections are concluded.
Next, I shall clarify the extent to which the various afflictions (*kleśa*) moisten rebirth.
Regarding this, there is no definitive judgment in the sūtras and śāstras;
however, for now, I shall discuss it according to the underlying principles.
Among the nine grades of afflictions, the first two grades and the five grades of discernment are both "superior-superior" (adhimātrādhimātra);
because their categories are identical, they equally moisten three lifetimes.
Among these, the first grade alone moistens three births;
the remaining fetters assist in moistening fourteen births;
and among those, the last grade alone moistens three births.
The remaining fetters assist and moisten eleven births.
How is this known?
It is because the fetters of the third and fourth categories each moisten two births.
These first two categories are coarse compared to those fetters;
therefore, they moisten three lifetimes.
Being adjacent to them, they cannot exceed three.
Furthermore, the remaining categories combine into two groups;
these two groups are equal in their capacity to moisten rebirth.
Following this pattern, the first two groups likewise moisten three lifetimes.
Question: These two [karmas] equally moisten three lifetimes;
what is the difference between them?
In the initial stage, the afflictions are coarse and intense, so rebirth occurs swiftly;
in the subsequent stage, the afflictions are subtle, so rebirth occurs slowly.
It is like a person who, upon seeing an object, greedily and rapidly seizes it when the desire is strong, but takes it only after a delay when the desire is slight.
Furthermore, the first category involves coarse afflictions and the resulting retribution is coarse and inferior;
the subsequent categories involve subtle afflictions and the resulting retribution is refined and superior.
Moreover, the first category is coarse, forceful, and powerful.
The moisture of meditative concentration (samādhi) can sustain three lifetimes; if it is inferior or thin in its subsequent stages,
it may sustain two lifetimes.
Alternatively, it moistens three lifetimes;
however, this is not stated as a definitive rule that they all moisten equally.
This statement regarding "three" is made from the perspective of the maximum limit.
Furthermore, the two categories and the five categories are both classified as "superior-middling.
Because their types are identical, they equally moisten two births;
among them, the first category alone moistens two births.
The remaining categories of karma, acting as mutual support, together moisten eight births;
the final category of karma alone moistens two births.
The remaining categories of karma, acting as mutual support, together moisten six births.
How is this known?
The first two chapters each moisten three lifetimes;
these two [chapters] are more subtle than those.
Therefore, there are not more than two.
Furthermore, the fifth and sixth grades each moisten one lifetime;
these two are coarser than those [preceding].
Therefore, the two are not few.
Furthermore, among those fourteen births, the first six births are moistened by the afflictions of the first and second categories.
Therefore, having severed the first and second grades of fetters (saṃyojana),
six births are eliminated and eight births remain.
As the treatise says:
If one has abandoned three or four grades of afflictions and will undergo two or three more births, this is called *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
Regarding "three births," this refers to three human births and three celestial births, totaling six births.
Regarding "two births," this refers to two human births and two celestial births, totaling four births.
In the remaining eight births, having severed the third grade of fetters that moisten rebirth and experiencing the remaining six births,
one is clearly known as a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
The third [type] moistens two births alone;
having severed the fetters that moisten birth for the fourth grade, they undergo four remaining births and are thus called *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
If one clearly knows this,
what is the difference between the fourth [dhyāna] alone moistening two births?
The distinctions are as explained previously.
The fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the fifth and sixth categories are combined;
these five categories of analysis are all likewise considered "strong" (*adhimātra*).
Because they are of a similar nature, they collectively moisten one birth;
among them, the first category alone moistens one birth,
while the remaining categories assist it to collectively moisten four births.
The conclusion of the final chapter alone moistens one lifetime,
while the remaining chapters provide assistance that together moisten three lifetimes;
such is the logical principle.
However, this single category possesses the sense of being "severed by the vehicle.
If it is severed by that vehicle, it does not serve to moisten rebirth;
if it is not yet severed by the vehicle, it may still serve to moisten rebirth.
Question: How is it known that each of these two moistens one lifetime?
In the previous two categories, each moistens two births;
this category is subtler than those,
moistening only one and no more.
The seventh and eighth [karmas] together moisten a single lifetime;
although this category is coarse compared to that,
it moistens one [life] without deficiency.

Furthermore, the treatise proclaims that one who has severed the fourth grade of the delusions that moisten rebirth and subsequently undergoes four more births is called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
Upon completing the abandonment of the fifth and sixth categories [of afflictions], one becomes a Sakṛdāgāmin;
it is clearly understood that only two more births remain.
Each of these two moistens one birth. Question:
Each of these two moistens one birth.
What is the difference?
It is as explained above regarding the afflictions of the seventh and eighth categories.
The five grades of distinction are collectively of the middle grade;
because their categories are identical, they together moisten one lifetime.
The remaining grades provide assistance, together moistening two lifetimes.
How is this known?
The two preceding categories each moisten one lifetime;
this category is subtler than those.
Therefore, the moisture is unified as one.
Furthermore, among the remaining two births of a Sakṛdāgāmin, if the seventh or eighth grade of fetters is severed, only one birth is reduced;
one birth still remains.
It is clearly known that these two together moisten a single lifetime. Question:
What is the distinction between these two, which together moisten a single lifetime?
The explanation states:
The former [karma] is coarse and its power to produce rebirth through moisture is strong;
the latter category is subtle and its power to produce rebirth through moisture is weak,
serving merely as an auxiliary.
Question: These two [defilements] together moisten a single birth.
When the seventh grade is severed, how can the eighth grade moisten that birth?
The commentary states:
It is not logically possible for the eighth [consciousness] alone to moisten half a lifetime.
If the seventh is severed, then that eighth category, together with the ninth, moistens one entire lifetime.
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:
"One who abandons the seventh grade [of afflictions] undergoes one more birth;
one who abandons the eighth grade likewise undergoes one more birth."
Those nine grades, when divided into five categories, constitute the inferior grade, which moistens only a single lifetime.
Question: For what reason do the seventh and eighth grades together moisten a single lifetime?
This stage is extremely subtle and moistens only a single lifetime;
because it binds one at the point of death,
once this has been transcended, there is no further place of rebirth.
Because it competes in strength and is firmly bound, it alone moistens one [thing].
Question: The Abhidharma says:
The srotāpanna relies on the future dhyāna (anāgāmya-dhyāna) to enter the noble path.
Since the afflictions to be abandoned in reliance upon that future dhyāna ought to be counteracted,
how can there still be the nine grades of full fetters remaining to moisten rebirth?
The commentary states:
It is not necessarily the case that all future dhyānas (anāgāmya-dhyāna) can remedy the fetters (saṃyojana).
This is provided that one has already previously cultivated and attained the future dhyāna.
By practicing the contemplation of the six aspects, one is able to sever the fetters;
if one does not do so, all the fetters remain intact.
Therefore, although the Srotāpanna relies on the future [dhyāna] to enter the Noble Path, [the fetters are severed].
It is not precluded that there may be a connection [of karma] that moistens rebirth.
A question is asked:
The *Tattvasiddhi* proclaims:
A *srotāpanna* must rely on the seven stages of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), to enter the Noble Path.
At the time of attaining those concentrations, they suppress and sever the fetters of desire (*kāma-saṃyojana*).
Having attained the state of a *srotāpanna*, by what means do they sustain their rebirth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and receive a body there?
Some explain that this is because one uses the afflictions previously arisen in the past to moisten birth and receive a body; however,
this interpretation is incorrect.
Although there was a past, it does not function in the present;
since one has no craving for objects,
how could one receive a body?
Others further say:
"In that school, the Noble Ones do not fall away from the Noble Path, but they can fall away from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Because of this falling away from concentration, they give rise to the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that moisten rebirth."
If that were so, those *srotāpannas* who are fixed in non-retrogression should necessarily be reborn in the higher realms;
however, the sūtras and śāstras do not permit such rebirth for *srotāpannas*.
This is clearly understood.
Rebirth in the lower realms does not result from falling back from meditative absorption;
this is now being explained.
Among the afflictions of the desire realm, there are infinite degrees of coarseness and subtlety.
The concentrations capable of subduing [defilements] range from the stage of an ordinary person to that of a Buddha, with countless distinctions between them.
The concentration based upon the *srotāpanna* is coarse and shallow;
it merely subdues the coarse categories of afflictions, while subtle afflictions still persist.
Within the subtle afflictions, they are divided into nine grades according to their meaning;
these are employed to moisten rebirth.
This is the third [category] regarding the extent of that moisture for rebirth.
Next, the fourth section clarifies the extent to which afflictions are abandoned and births are curtailed.
Within this, there are two sub-sections of analysis.
The first clarifies the differences in the abandonment [of afflictions].
Second, the impairment is explained in terms of abandonment.
There are two kinds of abandonment:
first, sequential and distinct abandonment.
Second is "successive abandonment" (*anupūrva-prahāṇa*).
The gradual pacification and gradual abandonment of the afflictions according to their coarseness or subtlety is called "distinct abandonment.
Because the subsequent stages are abandoned by means of the preceding stages being eliminated, it is termed "successive abandonment."
Among the nine grades of afflictions, the sixth grade is definitively severed by the vehicle.
Why is this so? Because upon the exhaustion of these afflictions, one realizes the second fruit, that of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
Because the aspiration for the fruit is so intense,
one necessarily relies on the sixth [moment] to abandon the fifth;
this principle of relying on a higher stage to abandon a lower one is largely consistent across all treatises.
Regarding the ninth category, there are differing opinions among the commentators.
In the *Vibhāṣā*, one master states that this is also abandoned by means of the vehicle (*yāna*).
Therefore, that text states:
"If the eighth grade [of affliction] were severed, then the ninth grade would be unable to obstruct;
why, then, must this grade be severed in succession?"
The meaning is the same as explained previously.
In this stage, the defilements are exhausted and the fruit of *anāgāmin* is realized;
thus, the aspiration for the fruit is intense.
It is severed by this vehicle.
If one relies on the Abhidharma, it is certainly not severed by the vehicle;
because at the very end of life it acts as an obstacle, one does not ride upon it.
Just as when guarding someone returning, the restraint is lax before they reach the border,
but it becomes strict once they arrive at the border;
therefore, this is the meaning.
If one has already transcended these [stages], in what place would one take rebirth?
Therefore, it is difficult for the vehicle to be interrupted.
As for the remaining seven grades, they are abandoned gradually according to their respective distinctions; in all cases, there is no sense of a "vehicle" [to be interrupted].
Some say that the second and eighth [stages] are also vehicles for abandonment. Why is this so?
Because the mind is empowered by the rest it finds after the fruit,
one must necessarily rely on the second [path] to abandon the first [defilement],
and rely on the eighth [path] to abandon the seventh grade [of defilement].
This interpretation is incorrect.
If there were those among the second category who could sever the vehicle, the sūtras and śāstras should have mentioned it;
yet there is no mention of such a case anywhere.
Knowing this clearly,
one does not mount it;
furthermore, the eighth chapter of the treatise discusses not mounting.
By analogy with what follows,
one clearly understands that the second [type] is not a vehicle for severance.
The *Vibhāṣā* states:
"If the seventh [category of afflictions] is severed, then that eighth category, together with the ninth category, jointly moisten one lifetime.
This clearly demonstrates [the point].
Chapter Eight: Non-Vehicle Severance.
Question: As was stated previously:

Regarding those who attain liberation through the vehicle of abandonment (*yāna-prahāṇa*): does this mean that the continuity [of defilements] is severed and exhausted through a single contemplation, which is called "liberation through the vehicle"?
Or does it mean that they are definitively severed and exhausted within a single lifetime, which is called "liberation through the vehicle"?
The commentary states:
The complete exhaustion of a single lifetime’s determinate [defilements] is called "vehicle-exhaustion" (yāna-prahāṇa);
it is not the case that the continuous exhaustion of a single meditative observation is called "vehicle-exhaustion."
Furthermore, that which is exhausted without interruption in the present life is also called "vehicle-exhaustion" (*yāna-kṣaya*).
That which is distinguished as exhaustion [at a specific time] is also called "vehicle-exhaustion";
it is not exhausted within a single lifetime.
When [the defilements] are employed, one receives a body;
they are severed only after passing through births, and thus this is not called "severance by means of a vehicle. Such is the meaning of severance.
Next, regarding the explanation of impairment through abandonment:
by abandoning the first category [of afflictions], one impairs three of the fourteen births;
by abandoning the second category, one further impairs three births.
There are only eight births remaining; by abandoning the third category [of afflictions], two births are eliminated, leaving six births remaining:
three as a human and three as a deva.
Having abandoned the fourth category, one further reduces two more births;
there remain four births:
two as a human and two as a deva.
Therefore, the treatise states:

"If one abandons three or four categories [of afflictions], having two or three more births remaining, this is called 'one who goes from family to family' (kulaṃkula). Having abandoned the fifth category, and by means of that abandonment, further diminishing two births, one proceeds."
Two [births] remain.
Having severed seven [births] or eight [births], one further diminishes one birth;
thus, one birth remains.
When the ninth grade [of afflictions] is severed, one further birth is eliminated and everything is exhausted.
Such is the extent of the bodies received by a *srotāpanna*. These two sections are concluded. Next, the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) is explained.
Within this section, there are four gates of analysis:
first, a general explanation of the meaning of *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family);
second, an elucidation of the intended meaning of the teaching.
The third [section] establishes the reason for the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner;
the fourth [section] analyzes its presence or absence in relation to other fruits.
First, regarding the general explanation of the meaning of "family-to-family":
The commentary’s own explanation states:
"Because one goes from family to family, it is called 'family-to-family' (kulaṃkula).
This clarifies that a *srotāpanna* who has become weary of their former place of birth and receives a body in a different family is thus named "family-to-family."
What is meant by "other families"?
Such a person may at times be born among humans, then pass away from the human state and be reborn in the heavens;
subsequently, passing away from that celestial body, they are again reborn among humans.
One grows weary of one's place of birth and takes rebirth in another family;
it is the same among the devas:
one leaves one's place of birth and takes rebirth in another location.
Therefore it is said that they are in different places.
A question is asked:
If one who receives a body in these different places is called a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner, [then...]
Why does the treatise state that they exist among humans—
either in one place, or two, or three— or among devas—
either in one heaven, or two, or three?
The commentary states:
among humans, "one family" may refer to a single household, or a single *jia* (clan), or a single royal house; these are termed "one family."
In all such cases, it does not preclude the fact that individual families may differ from one another;
the same applies to the heavens.
Among the six heavens, or within a single celestial realm,
there is no impediment to their dwelling in various distinct locations;
therefore, they are called "from family to family" (kulaṃkula).
The first section is thus concluded.
Next, the intention behind proclaiming the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner is clarified;
in order to manifest its excellence, the treatise states:
The "Srotāpanna who excels" is called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
How is this excellence manifested?
Among those who have entered the stream (*srotāpanna*), their fetters (*saṃyojana*) vary in degree—some are thick and others are thin.
Those whose fetters are thick do not abandon their former abodes and may cause [the defilements] to arise again;
thus, they are not called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
Therefore, the bodies received through the first, second, and third grades of fetters are not subsumed under the category of "family-to-family."
Those who are "thin" (mṛdu) are not like this;
they are unwilling to be reborn again.
Because they are distinguished as being "thin" rather than "thick" (adhimātra), they are called *kulaṃkula* ("one who goes from family to family").
The explanation of the mind is thus.
Next, the meaning of establishing the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) is clarified;
it is established based on three meanings as found in the treatises.
First, the severance of afflictions;
second, the accomplishment of the untainted faculties;
third, the taking of birth.
The phrase "severing afflictions" distinguishes [the practitioner] from those who possess only a slight degree of the Srotāpanna;
"attaining the untainted faculties" distinguishes them from those subject to regression,
and also distinguishes them from ordinary worldlings.
The term "rebirth" (upapatti) is used to distinguish [this type of practitioner] from those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin), such as the srotāpanna and others.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"If one has abandoned three or four categories [of afflictions] and has accomplished their antidote..."
Those who have two or three more births remaining are called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
The first meaning is that they have abandoned three or four categories [of afflictions].
Alternatively, they may have abandoned nine categories, or three categories, of the afflictions.
Or [he] may sever four grades.
Question: For what reason must one sever these afflictions specifically to be called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family)?
Among the nine grades of afflictions, the first three are coarse and heavy;

because the feeling of aversion toward one's previous place of birth is slight, they may cause rebirth there, and thus do not conform to the definition of a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).
This is because one must first sever [the defilements] to become a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.
Question: If it is said that the first three categories of afflictions are coarse, then for those who have been born into a previous family and are to be reborn again, [how is this explained]?
One should be reborn simultaneously among both humans and devas.
Why is it that one must necessarily be born from the human realm into the deva realm, and from the deva realm necessarily into the human realm? Thus he explained.
When one is born into this present life,
one truly perceives its suffering: one who loathes humanity seeks the heavens,
and one who loathes the heavens seeks humanity.
For this reason, they are not combined;
coarse fetters shroud the mind,
and after a long time, one returns to craving.
Therefore, one attains rebirth.
Question: Among those nine grades of afflictions, three are abandoned and four are applied.
One who has severed four [fetters] and exercises five [applications] is likewise called a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
Why is it not said that one who has severed five [fetters] and exercises six [applications], or one who has severed six [fetters] and exercises seven or eight [applications], is a "family-to-family"?
The commentary states:
Having severed the five [lower fetters], one necessarily mounts the sixth;
because one does not undergo rebirth [in the desire realm], this is not a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner.
In the seventh and eighth stages, one receives no distinct bodies among humans or devas;
therefore, these are not "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) practitioners. This establishes the second meaning of their antidote.
This refers to the uncontaminated antidotes that counteract three grades and four grades of fetters.
Even ordinary worldlings can sever these three and four grades of fetters, yet they are not "those who go from family to family" (kulaṃkula).
Therefore, it is necessary to explain these other two births and three births;
this is the meaning of the third type of rebirth.
Regarding "the other two births," there are two human births and two celestial births, which together constitute four births.
Regarding those who undergo three more births: the three human and three celestial births together constitute six births.
Among the nine grades of afflictions, one who has abandoned the first three grades uses the fourth grade to undergo those six births.
Having severed the fourth grade [of afflictions], one undergoes four births by means of the fifth grade.
The *srotāpanna* who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life possesses the former two meanings [of being a "family-to-family" practitioner] but does not undergo further births;
because he does not become a "family-to-family" practitioner (*kulaṃkula*), this must be explained.
This concludes the third section, which clarifies the establishment of the meaning of "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
Next, we shall examine its presence or absence in relation to other fruits.
A question is asked:
Why is it that among the fruits [of the path], the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) is specifically mentioned for the first fruit, while the other fruits are not?
The explanation states:
because within the realms of humans and devas, those in the first fruit undergo many births through coming and going.
There is the principle of "from house to house," which is why it is specifically mentioned;
the others lack this principle.
This shall not be discussed here.
A question is asked:
"Does the Anāgāmin also receive many bodies within the higher realms?"
Why is it not stated? Because the meaning of immeasurable births does not apply to each of those individual locations;
therefore, this is not the case for a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner. Thus ends the section on these four gates.
Next, regarding the *srotāpanna*, their capacities are distinguished as sharp or dull;
the classification is indeterminate,
sometimes divided into two.
There are only those who are sharp and those who are dull,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.

That text distinguishes between the sharp and the dull based on those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*) and those who do so after taking rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*).
Manifesting parinirvāṇa is for the sake of benefiting others.
Regarding those who take birth among humans, from two births up to many, they are generally considered dull-witted;
one birth is not taken into account.
Why is it not discussed?

Because among those born in a single lifetime, there are both those of combined capacities and those who are either dull or sharp; since it is difficult to definitively determine them as one or the other, it is not mentioned.
In what sense are they "of combined capacity"?
There are those who ought to attain nirvāṇa in the present life,
yet are obstructed by other conditions or lack the necessary provisions.
Alternatively, one may be unable to attain it due to the hindrance of illness and lack of strength that obstructs the cultivation of the path; consequently,
one must wait until after passing through a birth to finally attain it.
This is indeed a benefit.
There are those who, though diligently practicing in the present life,
do not attain it until after passing through successive births.
This, however, is dull.
Because it is indeterminate in this way, he did not mention it;
or else, it is divided into three.
Regarding sharp, dull, and middling faculties:
among the four types of persons listed above,
those who manifest parinirvāṇa in the present life are categorized as "sharp" based on their general characteristics and coarse classification.
Regarding the two intermediate types currently discussed as being of medium capacity, the Sūtra on Rebirth speaks of the *srotāpanna* as being dull-witted.
To discuss this in further detail: even among those currently categorized as of medium capacity, there are those who are dull-witted.
Although one may attain the stage of *anāgāmin* in the present life and only attain *nirvāṇa* after many births in the higher realms, there are also those who,
even after passing through births among humans, possess such benefit.
Although they do not attain further fruits in the present life, [they still possess this potential].
Having taken birth in the desire realm, one attains nirvana swiftly in the subsequent body.

Alternatively, it may be divided into six types: those who fall back (*parihāṇadharman*), those who attain through reflection (*cetana-dharman*), those who protect themselves (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those who abide in their state (*sthitākampya*), those who excel (*prativedhanādharman*), and those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*). The meanings of these are explained as follows.
If subdivided further according to their specific distinctions, they would likewise be immeasurable;
such is the case with the *srotāpanna*.
Next, the meaning of the *sakṛdāgāmin* will be explained in detail.
The candidate for the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin-patipanna) is generally termed Sakṛdāgāmin;
they are discussed together as one category.
Within this, there is a detailed analysis according to four gates.
First, determining its essence;
second, discerning its characteristics; third, distinguishing between the sharp and the dull faculties.
The fourth clarifies the extent of the severance of fetters.
Regarding the essential nature of the meditative state:
the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin takes the noble virtue as its essence.
The noble virtues are not uniform;
they likewise comprise three types.
The first is the essence of the fruit.
According to the Abhidharma’s analysis of cultivation,
only the sixth and final grade of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) among the nine grades of antidotes within the desire realm is taken as the essential substance of the fruit.
The untainted qualities of the fruit of Srotāpanna, as comprised by the analytical cultivation of the supernormal powers,
together with the untainted qualities within the stage of the candidate for Sakṛdāgāmin,
are combined to constitute the essence of the fruit.
What is the meaning of this?
When the resultant mind manifests, one relinquishes the previous acquisitions (*prāpti*).
Instead, there arises a distinct kind of acquisition of the result that is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*), which manifests at present.
One attains the mind of the sixth stage of the path of liberation,
and together with all the previously attained untainted states,
these are combined into a single fruit: the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
If one follows the *Tattvasiddhi*, it establishes only the cultivation of practice (*pratipatti-bhāvanā*) and does not speak of the cultivation of attainment (*prāpti-bhāvanā*);
therefore, it states that only the mind of the sixth and final liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*) constitutes the essence of the fruit.
All others have already passed away or do not currently exist as substantial entities;
therefore, they are not said to be results.
Such is the detailed analysis.
The cause of the theory of continuity fulfills the result.
The meaning of the two trainings and right view is the same as the previous explanation.
Third is the path of superior fruition (*viśeṣa-mārga*).
By further cultivating superior resolve (*adhimokṣa*), one progressively abandons seven, eight, or nine grades of afflictions;
this consists of three paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
This is called the "Supreme Fruit.
This concludes the first section.
Next, its characteristics will be explained.
This Sakṛdāgāmin is distinguished into three types:
first, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life by cultivating and realizing the fruit of arhatship in this very body;
second, one who progresses in the present life.
First, those who manifest their bodies and attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*, receiving rebirth in the higher realms;
second, those who pass through successive births;
and third, those who manifest without interval and receive rebirth in the desire realm.
These three types of separation can also be described as five.
There are two kinds of *sābhisamaya-parinirvāṇa*: first, the one who attains parinirvāṇa immediately upon manifestation.
First, having cultivated the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin within an ordinary body,
one attains parinirvāṇa in that very lifetime.
Second, one who undergoes rebirth.
Some may pass through births within the fruit of srotāpanna;
some may pass through births within the practice of sakṛdāgāmin,
and further attain the state of sakṛdāgāmin.
He entered parinirvāṇa in that very same body.
Counting the present [attainment] as one,
together with the preceding two, there are three.
Among those who undergo rebirth, there are two types.
The first is one who maintains the fruit;
this is called "once-returner."
Second is the "one who is progressing," called the "single-seeded" (ekabījika).
This single-seeded person is also established by way of three causes and conditions.
That is to say:
the severance of afflictions, the accomplishment of the antidotes, the untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*),
and rebirth in higher realms.
The commentary explains that if even one of these three is missing, it is not a single seed.
Combining this with the preceding [categories], they are collectively stated as five.
The differentiation of characteristics is thus; these two gates are concluded.
Next, the distinction between the sharp and the dull faculties is analyzed, wherein the opening and closing [of categories] are not fixed.
To summarize, there are only two types:
namely, the sharp-witted and the dull-witted.
Those who manifest parinirvāṇa are of sharp faculties;
the others are of dull faculties.
This is also acceptable.
Those who have been born through successive lifetimes consider this [wisdom] to be dull; others call it "beneficial.
Alternatively, it is divided into three types.
That is to say:
among those of sharp, dull, and middling faculties, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life is of sharp faculty.
Those who manifest progress are classified as medium;
those who undergo rebirth are classified as dull.
Such is the coarse judgment.
To speak according to the actual facts, among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin), there are likewise those of sharp and dull faculties.
One who attains parinirvāṇa directly is described as being of sharp faculties,
while one who attains parinirvāṇa after being reborn [once more] is considered to be of dull faculties.
Among those currently progressing toward the state of a human, there are also those of sharp and dull faculties.

Among those progressing toward the state of an Anāgāmin, one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state is of sharp faculties, while one who is reborn in the higher realms is of dull faculties.
Even among those born as humans, there are both the sharp and the dull;
one type is sharp, while the other type is dull.
Alternatively, they may be divided into six:

the meanings of falling back (*parihāṇi*), reflection (*cetanā*), guarding (*anurakṣaṇā*), abiding (*sthiti*), advancing (*viśeṣagamana*), and immovability (*akopya*) are determined as follows at the conclusion of these three sections.
Next, the extent to which the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned by a *sakṛdāgāmin* is explained.
The Sūtra states:
"The Sakṛdāgāmin eliminates the three fetters and attenuates greed, hatred, and delusion.
The meaning of "eliminating the three fetters" has been explained above.

These are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Because these were previously severed [at the stage of the stream-enterer], they are mentioned collectively here as being absent.
Furthermore, these three also possess the sense of being partially severed by the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
As explained later,
that which is called "thin" refers precisely to greed,
hatred, and delusion as the objects to be abandoned.
To what extent has it been attenuated?
Among the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm,
the Sakṛdāgāmin who maintains the fruit has eliminated six grades, leaving three remaining.
This is called "thinness.
One who progresses toward the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin abandons seven or eight categories [of afflictions],
or abandons nine categories without yet having realized liberation.
In the past, when discussing this, it was called "thin";
the severing of fetters is thus.
Among these, there are meanings identical to those of the *srotāpanna*.
The preceding cases may be understood by analogy;
there is no need for further explanation.
It is the same for the Sakṛdāgāmin.
Next, the meaning of *anāgāmin* will be explained individually.
The term *anāgāmin* is used as a general designation for those who are candidates for arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*),
as they are discussed together in this single section.
Within this, there is also a fourfold analysis:
first, determining its essence;
second, distinguishing its characteristics.
Third, the distinction between those of dull and sharp faculties;
fourth, the degree to which the fetters of desire have been severed.
As for the essential nature of meditative concentration:
The fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala) has noble virtue as its essence.
There are three aspects to this noble virtue:
the first is the essence of the fruit itself.

According to the Abhidharma, regarding the cultivation of the analytical meditation on the stages of practice, the fruit-body consists solely of the single moment of untainted liberation at the very end of the antidote for the nine grades of the desire realm.
The cultivation of analytical supernormal knowledge subsumes all preceding untainted states and unifies them as the essence of the fruit.
What is the meaning of this?
At the moment of realizing the state of Anāgāmin,
one first attains the complete abandonment [of the defilements]. This consists of the final liberation within the nine grades of antidotes for the desire realm acquired through birth,
as well as all preceding untainted (anāsrava) attainments.
These are combined into a single fruit.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, only the cultivation through practice (*caryā-bhāvanā*) is established, and there is no meaning of cultivation through attainment (*prāpti-bhāvanā*).
Therefore, it is taught that only the final liberation within the antidote to the desire realm constitutes the essence of the fruit.
Second is the path of training and equal vision;
its meaning is the same as explained previously.
Third is the path of superior fruit.
He further cultivates superior practices,
progressively severing the fetters from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
he attains liberation solely at the very end of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This is called the "Exalted Fruit" (*viśeṣaphala*).
These three are collectively designated as the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
Such is the definitive nature [of this fruit]. This concludes the first section.
Next, their characteristics are distinguished.
Among the Anāgāmins, the categories of opening and closing are not fixed;
they are explained by increasing the number.
In brief, there are only three types.
The first is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*): having cultivated the path in this very body, they attain the fruit of arhatship and enter parinirvāṇa.

Second is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, because such a person, having ascended from the desire realm, takes birth in the intermediate state between the two realms and attains parinirvāṇa there, they are called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state."
Because that treatise does not establish the doctrine of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*),

it relies on other sūtras and śāstras to define "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" as one who attains parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state body while ascending from the desire realm to the higher realms. This is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyī*).
There are three types of parinirvāṇa regarding the body:
attaining parinirvāṇa after receiving a body in the upper realms.
Alternatively, they may be divided into four.
First, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon manifestation;
second, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state; third, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of form.
One attains nirvana while in a body within the form realm;
one attains nirvana through the four formless attainments within the formless realm.
Alternatively, they are divided into six,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*: first, the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*).
Second, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state;
third, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth;
fourth, those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion.
Fifth is the one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin); sixth is the one who flows upwards (ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāyin).
Regarding the first, the one who attains parinirvāṇa upon manifestation (abhisamaya-parinirvāyin), there are three causes and conditions.
The reason for manifesting parinirvāṇa is that,
possessing sharp faculties, one perceives the faults of the afflictions and swiftly eliminates them;
this is why one manifests parinirvāṇa.
Second, having attained the Noble Path, they have already developed a deep-seated aversion toward the suffering of birth in the desire realm;
fearing birth in the higher realms, they diligently cultivate the remedies.
Therefore, they attain parinirvāṇa in the present life.
Third, there are those who attain future dhyāna and,
relying upon it, sever the fetters;
although they have attained the other dhyānas, these do not manifest before them.
In the two higher realms, there is neither the karma of action nor the karma of birth.
For this reason, one attains parinirvāṇa in the present life. Among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, there are two causes and conditions.
First, because the noble path manifests within the intermediate state (antarābhava) for those of sharp faculties,
they are able to swiftly see the faults of the afflictions and eliminate them; therefore,
they attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Because of their sharp faculties, they attain parinirvāṇa therein.
Second, there is the classification according to karma.
Karma is of two kinds:
first, karma that produces action;
second, karma that brings about rebirth.
That which arises from afflictions is called "karma of action.
If the activity of afflictions is moistened by craving and is able to produce a future result,
it is called "karma of rebirth."
This person has cultivated and attained the eight worldly dhyānas, which possess their respective karmic functions;
yet, because they have no craving for these dhyānas, they lack the karma for rebirth. Thus, they attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin).
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Sentient beings in the realms of desire and form have two kinds of karma:
first, the karma of action (*kriyā-karman*)."
Second is the karma for taking birth.
Those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possess only the karma of formation; therefore, they enter parinirvāṇa therein.
Question: Since this person possesses sharp faculties,
why does he not attain parinirvāṇa in the present life or attain it upon reaching the middle of the path?
As explained in the commentary on *nirvāṇa*,
although this person possesses sharp faculties, their four great elements are so weak and inferior that they are incapable of practicing the Path;
or, though they possess strength, their supporting conditions are insufficient.
Because of this, one cannot attain nirvana in the present life.
It is asked: Is it only those of extremely sharp faculties who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?
There are also gradations of difference,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
there are superior, middling, and inferior [levels].
If there are those of superior faculties with mild afflictions,
they attain parinirvāṇa without having yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire.
If there are those of middling faculties with middling afflictions, [they attain parinirvāṇa after being born once more].
One who has just departed from the desire realm but has not yet reached the form realm attains parinirvāṇa;
however, if one possesses inferior faculties and superior afflictions,
they attain nirvāṇa only upon reaching the limits of the form realm.
Question: For what reason is there *nirvāṇa* within the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas it does not exist in the higher realms?
This shall be explained by analyzing the four meanings of *nirvāṇa*.
First, explaining according to nature:
sentient beings of the desire realm possess a courageous and robust nature capable of attaining the fruits of the path;
therefore, it is said that there is nirvana within the desire realm.
The higher realms are not like this, and therefore there is no intermediate parinirvāṇa (*antarāparinirvāṇa*).
Second, the explanation is given in terms of the causes and conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*):
the afflictions of the desire realm have two causes and conditions.
There are two types: internal and external.
That which gives rise to afflictions by not severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), as well as improper reflection (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), is called internal.
The six sense objects give rise to fetters;
these are designated as "external.
Both of these are to be loathed.
Therefore, there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In the higher realms, there are only internal causes that give rise to fetters (*saṃyojana*), and no external objects to be loathed;
thus, there is no parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state there.
Third, the analysis and explanation are made in relation to two types of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
There are two kinds of craving:
first, craving for sensual desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*).
First, attachment to the external requisites for life consisting of the five sensual desires;
second, craving for form, which is the attachment to the beauty of one's wife.
Because these [coarse afflictions] exist within the stages of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there is "attainment of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyī) therein;
because these do not exist in the higher realms, there is no such attainment there.
This fourth point is explained by way of distinguishing the various coarse afflictions (paryavasthāna).

In the desire realm, there exist coarse afflictions such as stinginess, greed, anger, envy, lack of shame, and lack of remorse, which can be objects of revulsion; therefore, there is "attainment of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarāparinirvāyin).
In the higher realms, these do not exist, and thus there is no attainment of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
Question: The Sūtra states that there are four types of mental states for one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin).
What are they? As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
first, the mind that is neither in training (*śaikṣa*) nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That is to say, the mind that takes rebirth;
second, the mind of training,
which gives rise to superior counteractive measures.
Third, the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣacitta),
which realizes the fruit of arhatship.
Fourth, the mind that is neither in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣacitta).
This refers to the mind at the moment of death. Question:
With what kind of mind does this person die?
The treatise itself states:
"The retributive mind and the deportment mind of an Arhat conform to the mind that is tending toward cessation and proceed toward Nirvana.
Among these four types of minds, two are Nirvana.
The second is not nirvāṇa.
Regarding "the two [types of] nirvāṇa," these refer to the latter two minds.
The third, the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), is the mind that realizes *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder).

The fourth, which is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, is the mind that enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. The case of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) is likewise.

Next, the [attainments of] one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), with exertion (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*), and without exertion (*anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin*) shall be explained.
These three types of persons possess karma for their activities and karma for rebirth that results in taking birth in the upper realms;
within the levels of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are divided into three according to the principle of the first place of birth among whichever heavens they may inhabit.
It is not restricted to the first dhyāna.
How do these three differ?
The sūtras and śāstras do not agree on this point.
Furthermore, there are three distinctions.

According to the Abhidharma, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin) are the most excellent; those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion (abhisamskāra-parinirvāyin) are next.
"Non-practice is the most inferior.
What is the meaning of this?
The treatise itself explains:
One who practices with diligent application and cultivates the path of swift progress is one born in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin).
There is also one who possesses diligent application but lacks the path of swift progress.

This is the one who attains parinirvāṇa through application (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin). One who lacks diligent means and lacks the path of swift progress is the one who attains parinirvāṇa without application (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin).
Diligently cultivating the noble path is called "diligent application" (*vīrya-upāya*);
because of one's sharp faculties, what is cultivated is swiftly accomplished.
Rapidly severing the remaining fetters is called the "path of swift progress."
For what reason is this person called "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*)?
The treatise itself explains:
"This person, immediately upon being born, gives rise to the path of practice."

Because they swiftly sever the remaining fetters through diligent application of skillful means and attain parinirvāṇa upon their first birth, they are called "attainers of parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin).
Cultivating the sixteen noble practices that are untainted is called the path with remainder.
One attains parinirvāṇa with remainder at birth,
and only upon the exhaustion of one’s lifespan does one attain parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Some say that one attains parinirvāṇa without remainder immediately upon birth;
this interpretation is not correct.
The treatise states:
"Because there is no relinquishing of the life-faculties (*āyus-saṃskāra*).
As for the second person, who diligently cultivates the path, this is called 'diligent application' (*vīryopāya*)."
Because of dull faculties, that which is cultivated is difficult to accomplish;
because they sever the fetters not quickly, it is called the "path without speed.
For what reason is such a person called one who attains parinirvāṇa upon going (abhisamskāraparinirvāyin)?
The commentary’s own explanation states:
One who gives rise to the path with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra-mārga*) to sever the fetters and attain parinirvāṇa is called one who attains parinirvāṇa through effort (*abhisamskāraparinirvāyin*).

Furthermore, one who relies on a conditioned meditative concentration (*saṃskṛta-pratyaya-samādhi*) to sever the fetters and attain parinirvāṇa is also called one who attains parinirvāṇa through effort.
This person also cultivates the sixteen noble practices, which is called the path with outflows.
Furthermore, because this person possesses sharp faculties, they contemplate the conditioned phenomena of the first three truths.
They are also able to sever the fetters; thus they are called "conditioned by existence" (*bhavāśrita*).
Because they lack the swift path for severing the fetters, they do not proceed rapidly, but only attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan.
The third person is unable to diligently practice the Noble Path, which is called "not seeking with diligence";
nor can they swiftly sever the remaining fetters, which is called "lacking the swift path."
For what reason is this person named "one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion" (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin)?
The treatise itself explains:
because they attain parinirvāṇa by giving rise to the path of non-exertion (*anabhisamskāra-mārga*) to sever their fetters, they are named "one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion."
Furthermore, based on the concentration of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as a condition, one severs the fetters and attains parinirvāṇa; this is also called "without exertion" (anabhisamskāra).
Such a person possesses dull faculties and primarily uses contaminated knowledge (sāsrava-jñāna) and the like to sever the fetters.
Not cultivating the sixteen noble practices of the untainted is called the "path of non-action.
Even if one cultivates the untainted to sever the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
because of dull faculties, one contemplates the unconditioned, supreme dharma of the truth of cessation.
Only when one is able to sever the fetters can it be called "conditioned by the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-pratisaṃyukta*).
Because there is no swift path for the rapid severing of fetters, one attains parinirvāṇa only at the end of one's lifespan.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, birth-parinirvāṇa (*upapadya-parinirvāṇa*) is superior.
The one who attains parinirvāṇa through effort is inferior to the one who attains it without effort.
As for the second person, he knows for himself that he will certainly attain nirvāṇa.
One who does not diligently practice the path but attains parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan is called one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin).
As for the third type of person, because they possess dull faculties, they attain it by diligently practicing the path.
One who attains parinirvāṇa at the end of their lifespan is called one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (abhisamskāraparinirvāyin).
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth, this is the most inferior; among those who attain parinirvāṇa through exertion, it is the most excellent.
Regarding "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion" (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin), what is the meaning of this?
Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth are called "those who attain parinirvāṇa with a body" (sopadhiśeṣa-parinirvāyin) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
This person, through diligent exertion throughout their entire life, attains parinirvāṇa upon receiving a body;
this is the most inferior [type].
This is identical to the person who attains parinirvāṇa through practice while established in the path.
Question: If one attains parinirvāṇa at the end of this life,
for what reason is it called "attaining parinirvāṇa while receiving a body"?
The Buddha himself explained:
"This person attains parinirvāṇa only after having received a body; this is called 'parinirvāṇa upon receiving a body.
It is not called 'parinirvāṇa upon receiving a body' because one attains parinirvāṇa at the very moment of first receiving a body."
There are those who, by the power of diligently cultivating samādhi, sever their fetters and attain parinirvāṇa before the end of their lifespan;
this is considered the most excellent [type of intermediate attainment], and it is the same as the "attainment of parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin) described in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
There are those who know for themselves that they will certainly attain nirvāṇa, yet through indolence fail to practice;
because of the power of conditioned samādhi, they attain parinirvāṇa at the end of their lives, which is called "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion" (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin).
Therefore, this constitutes the middle [type].
This is the same as the "non-practitioner" (aśaikṣa) in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Next, the "one who flows upward" (ūrdhva-srotas) is explained.
This person is of duller faculties.
Among those in the higher realms, one who does not attain parinirvāṇa in the first birth,
but only attains it from the second birth onward, is called an "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).
There are two kinds of streams:
first, the stream of afflictions;
second, the stream of the path.
The gradual arising of the abandonment of lower afflictions (*kleśa*) and the severing of higher fetters (*saṃyojana*) is called the "stream of affliction" (*kleśa-ogha*).
The progressive increase in the practice of the Path (*mārga*) is called the "stream of the Path" (*mārga-ogha*).
Because one ascends sequentially by means of these two streams, it is termed "ascending stream" (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Within this, there are briefly four types of distinctions.
First, the indeterminate *bhūmi*,
which has not yet reached the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*).
Within that state, some attain nirvana after receiving two or three bodies, etc.;
these are the two [types of] universal succession in receiving bodies.
First, by ascending as far as the Bṛhatphala heaven, one attains nirvāṇa.
Third, those who delight in wisdom are born in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Fourth is those who delight in concentration and are born in the formless realm.
These latter two types of persons differ from one another in their practice of the causes [of their respective states].
First, those who delight in discursive discussion; second, those who delight in tranquility.
Those who delight in the meaning of discourse are born in the five Pure Abodes;
those who delight in tranquility are born in the Formless Realm.
Furthermore, there are five stages.
Those who cultivate the permeating dhyāna (vāsana-dhyāna) are born in the five Pure Abodes;
those who do not cultivate the permeating dhyāna through these five stages are born in the Formless Realm.
What are these five stages of perfuming meditation?
They are: inferior, intermediate, superior, superior-intermediate, and supreme-superior.
What is perfumed meditation?
It is using untainted (anāsrava) meditation to perfume the tainted (sāsrava),
causing the tainted concentration to become refined, superior, and pure.
How is the method of perfuming practiced?
Having cultivated and attained the four dhyānas, the practitioner first perfumes the fourth dhyāna,
initially entering into many untainted (anāsrava) states of mind.
Next, one enters many contaminated states of mind,
and subsequently enters many uncontaminated states of mind;
thus, by alternating back and forth, one gradually abbreviates the process.
Continuing thus until the final two untainted minds and two tainted minds—
where the latter two untainted minds are called the preparatory path for perfuming dhyāna—
one subsequently enters into one untainted mind and one tainted mind.
Later, one untainted [attainment] is called "perfumed dhyāna.
Within this perfected state, one goes and returns five times;
the first return is termed "inferior."
Second rank among the middling;
third rank among the superior;
fourth rank among the superior-middling.
Fifth, the "superior-superior":
having perfumed the fourth dhyāna, one next perfumes the third dhyāna;
next, one perfumes the second dhyāna, and finally perfumes the first dhyāna.
The method of perfuming is entirely the same.
Having practiced the meditation of perfuming, if one does not regress, one will pass through five births in the Pure Abodes;
this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa upon rebirth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin).
They are not called "Upstreamers" (ūrdhvasrotas).
If there are those who regress, they are reborn in the heavens;
according to the number of their remaining faculties, they later sever their fetters once again.
Having attained the four dhyānas, one returns to re-impregnate them.
The method of impregnation is similar to the previous one.
Among those who have achieved this, those who impregnate it once are reborn in the Parīttābha Heaven (the Heaven of Limited Radiance).
It is also called "Free from Affliction" (Avṛha) and also called "Free from Worldlings" (Atapas).
Those who undergo two cycles of perfuming are born in the Heaven Free from Heat (Atapa).
Those who cultivate [the wholesome] three times are born in the Heaven of Good Visibility (Sudṛśa),
which is also called Good Appearance (Sudarśana).
Those who cultivate it four times are born in the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarsana).
Those who undergo five rounds of perfuming are born among the Śuddhāvāsa devas;
in foreign lands they are called Akaniṣṭha, which is the Ultimate of Form (Rūpakāyaparyanta).
Question: These five [factors] follow karma individually;
their moistening of delusion is likewise different.
The commentary states:
Although the specific karmas differ, the delusions they moisten are not distinct;
this is because these [karmas] belong to the same stage of bondage.
Just as among the six heavens of the desire realm, those born there share the same delusions but have different karma,
a question is asked:
"Are there persons who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) or who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) within these five Pure Abodes?"
To explain this according to one interpretation:
there are only those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadyaparinirvāyin), and none of the "those who go upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas). Why is this so?
Among the five stages of perfuming, one takes birth according to the superior [level],
because one does not first take birth in the lower and subsequently in the upper. Furthermore,
another interpretation states:
They may also attain their original state in a lower heaven.
Through the cultivation of inferior dhyāna, they are born in a lower heaven;
having been born in that heaven, they further cultivate superior cultivation and are born in a higher heaven.
Therefore, one attains the "Upstreamer" (ūrdhvasrotas).
If one can thus cultivate the five stages of dhyāna through perfuming, one will then feel revulsion toward and criticize the formless absorptions (ārūpya-samādhi),
and will not be reborn in the formless realms.
If one wishes to enter the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), one cannot cultivate the five stages of perfumed meditation (vāsanā-dhyāna).
These six types may likewise be divided into seven.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
there are six types as mentioned above, with the addition of the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (*ārūpya*).

What is the difference between this attainment of cessation in the formless realm (*ārūpya-nirodha-samāpatti*) and the previously mentioned meditative absorption of bliss (*sukha-samādhi*), such that it must be discussed separately?
The former absorption of bliss proceeds from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
this attainment of cessation in the formless realm proceeds from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because it differs from the preceding [classification], it is explained separately.
It can also be described as eightfold:
seven types are as previously stated.

Adding to this, there is the "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon going" (upapadyaparinirvāyin). This "one who attains parinirvāṇa upon going" is also the "one who goes upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas) among those in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu). As for the one who attains parinirvāṇa after being born there once:
it refers to one who, having been born in that [formless realm] for a single lifetime, immediately attains parinirvāṇa.

One who attains parinirvāṇa in the formless realm is called an "attainer of parinirvāṇa in the formless" (ārūpyopaga). One who attains parinirvāṇa only after having traversed two, three, or four bodily existences is called an "attainer of parinirvāṇa by going upward" (ūrdhvasrotas).
This has three stages.
As stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
first, there are those who possess diligence and mastery in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and thus receive two bodies;
second, there are those who possess diligence but lack mastery in meditative concentration.
If one possesses mastery in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but lacks diligence (*vīrya*), one receives three bodies.
If one lacks both diligence and mastery in meditative concentration,
and both matters are absent, then one receives four bodies.
In the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*),
there is no principle of rebirth; therefore, at most, one receives only four bodies, or divided, eleven.
As stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
first is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life;
second is the one who attains it after being reborn in another world.
Third is intermediate parinirvāṇa;
fourth is birth-parinirvāṇa; fifth is existence-parinirvāṇa.
Sixth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion;
seventh, one who delights in meditative concentration;
eighth, one who delights in wisdom.
Ninth, those liberated through faith;
tenth, those who have attained vision;
eleventh, those who have realized through the body.
The "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin) is one who, prior to being reborn,
unifies [the stages] into one; within that, specifically distinguished by practicing upon the basis of an ordinary body,
they attain the state of an Anāgāmin and subsequently attain nirvāṇa in that very same lifetime— this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life."
Regarding those who, having undergone rebirth in the desire realm within the body of a noble one (*ārya*),
subsequently attain the state of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*) and achieve *nirvāṇa* in that very same lifetime, these are described as "transmuted births" (*parivṛtta-jāti*).
This distinction exists because they have attained the state of a non-returner by transmuting their previous noble body.
Therefore, they are divided into two distinct groups.
Those who have transmigrated from the world of humans come from four places:
first, those who have come after passing through births following the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Second, those who come after having undergone rebirth while in the stage of practicing for the fruit of once-returning;
third, those who come after having undergone rebirth while in the stage superior to the fruit of once-returning;
fourth, those who come after having undergone rebirth while in the stage of practicing for the fruit of non-returning.

The first two [types of parinirvāṇa] are as previously explained. The intermediate-parinirvāṇa (antarāparinirvāyin), birth-parinirvāṇa (upapadyaparinirvāyin), with-effort-parinirvāṇa (sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin), and effortless-parinirvāṇa (anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin) are all explained exactly as before.
The two types—delight in concentration (samādhi-rata) and delight in wisdom (prajñā-rata)—are distinct classifications derived from within the category of those who ascend further (ūrdhvasrotas).
The names of the two upper realms have been established here.
The meaning is as explained above. Question:
It was previously stated that among those who ascend to the higher realms (ūrdhvasrotas), there are four types: namely,
those of indeterminate parinirvāṇa, those who attain nirvāṇa in all places, those with ease in concentration, and those with ease in wisdom.
Why does the *Tattvasiddhi* specifically highlight only the latter two?
This is because it does not exhaustively describe all cases, but rather discusses them according to their preeminence.
Since the causes and results of the latter two types of persons differ, they are singled out for mention.
Although these two categories encompass the *ūrdhvasrotas* (those who stream upward), they do not exhaust all cases.
If they are not exhaustive, where would those who are "not fixed" (*aniyata-parinirvāyin*) and those among the eleven types of persons belonging to all stages (*sarvatra-ga*) be included?
These are subsumed under the categories of faith-liberation (śraddhā-vimukti) and vision-attainment (dṛṣṭi-prāpta), because these two faculties universally encompass all [types of practitioners].
The preceding eight kinds are differentiated according to their physical basis, their conduct, and their meaning.
They are distinguished by their manifestation in the present life or at birth;
by their attainment of the goal while practicing or without further practice;
and by their inclination toward meditative concentration or wisdom, which distinguishes them according to their physical embodiment.
