The various types of those who undergo rebirth are distinguished according to their specific characteristics.
Among the first eight types of persons, those with dull faculties are called "liberated through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
Because they attain liberation by relying on the words of others,
those of sharp faculties are called "those who have attained vision through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
Because one sees phenomena with one's own mind and thereby attains liberation,
those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) are said to be "bodily witnesses" (kāyasākṣin).
For one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation, the mastery over the cessation of the mind is conjoined with the body.
Therefore, it is called "bodily realization.
There are eleven such types.
If one distinguishes them according to the faculties, stages, lineages, locations, degrees of detachment from desire, and so forth, they are immeasurable.
As stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya*,
the analysis of characteristics is thus concluded for these two gateways.
Next, there is the analysis and determination of the distinction between the sharp and dull faculties, as well as their opening and closing.
The essential classification is twofold:
namely, the sharp and the dull.
The dull are called those liberated through faith.
The views of gain and fame—
these two are pervasive throughout.

Regarding the coarse classification according to their characteristics, among the six types [of non-returners], those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth and those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state possess sharp faculties.
The others are of dull faculties.
Alternatively, they may be divided into three types, namely:
Within the categories of sharp and dull faculties, these are also designated as superior, middling, and inferior.

According to their distinct coarse divisions among the aforementioned six types, those who attain parinirvāṇa upon manifestation (abhisamaya-parinirvāyin) are the sharp, and those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) are the middling.
All others are termed "dull.
To speak according to the actual state of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, there are among them those who are sharp, dull, or middling;
yet, when one speaks of attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life in its direct sense, it is designated as "sharp."
Regarding rebirth in the existence of dullness and the existence of middleness:
when many lifetimes are transmigrated, it is called "dull";
when few, it is called "middling."
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin),
there are both those of sharp and dull faculties, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Tattvasiddhi*.
These are those who attain parinirvāṇa without having yet become detached from the desire realm.
This is called "benefit.
When one has just begun to leave the desire realm but has not yet reached the form realm, and attains parinirvāṇa therein,
this is described as "middling."
Those who attain parinirvāṇa only upon reaching the limits of the form realm (rūpadhātu) are said to be of dull faculties. Among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (upapadya-parinirvāyin),

those who attain it with effort (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin), and those who attain it without effort (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin), there are likewise distinctions of sharp, dull, and middling faculties.
Both are said to be indeterminate.

According to the Abhidharma, one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) is of sharp faculties, while one who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*) is of middling faculties.
Because non-exertion constitutes dullness,
it is said that one establishes birth-attainment (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*) based on sharp faculties and weak afflictions.
The "attainment of nirvana through effort" (sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) is established based on medium faculties and medium afflictions;
the "attainment of nirvana without effort" (anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin) is established based on dull faculties and superior afflictions;
and the "attainment of nirvana upon rebirth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin) is the most sharp when established based on the *Tattvasiddhi*.
It is similar to the previous case.
Among those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), the one who attains it through effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*) is of dull faculties.
If one proceeds toward parinirvāṇa based on practice, that is the most sharp;
proceeding without practice is middling;
and parinirvāṇa upon rebirth is dull.
All this has been explained above.
It should be understood that among those who attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream (ūrdhvasrotas), there are likewise distinctions between the sharp and the dull faculties,
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.
The first body is for the sake of benefit;
the second and third bodies are dull in all respects.
Furthermore, it is analyzed that they are not fixed as being for the benefit [of others],
but rather exist within all intermediate states.
Those who possess both dull concentration and dull wisdom are collectively termed "dull.
If one were to analyze further in detail, each of these categories contains internal distinctions of sharp, dull, and middling.
Alternatively, they may be further divided into six types of spiritual dispositions (*gotra*).
Reflecting on the possibility of falling back from, remaining in, or advancing toward immovability regarding the roots of goodness one has attained: that which can be lost is called "falling back.
One who is not already fallen, but through the application of reflection and aspiration is able to remain non-retrogressive, is called a "person of reflection" (cintāmayī-pudgala).
Fearing regression due to afflictions, one who constantly guards oneself and thus attains non-regression is called a person who upholds the Dharma through protection (*ārakṣaka-dharmika*).
One whose acquired roots of goodness neither regress nor advance is called a person who abides in the Dharma (*sthita-dharmika*).
The roots of goodness attained that are necessarily able to advance upward are called "certainly advancing.
The roots of goodness attained that are firm and do not regress are called "unshakable.
Among these, some are fundamentally unshakable.
Some may progress until they finally attain immovability (*akopya*).
According to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*), from those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life up to those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), all possess these six [types].
Such are the sharp and dull faculties; thus concludes this section on the three gates.
Next, the extent of the fetters severed by an Anāgāmin is clarified.
As stated in the sūtras,
one becomes an Anāgāmin by severing the five lower fetters, as well as the faults of shamelessness, lack of dread, stinginess, and envy.
What are the five fetters?
They are namely: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
The first three of these have already been severed and are no longer present.
Therefore, it is explained in general terms.
Furthermore, the first three [stages] also possess the sense of being directly severed by an Anāgāmin;
therefore, they are explained in general terms.
The meaning is as explained later.
The latter two [fetters] are exclusively abandoned by an Anāgāmin.
Among these five fetters, the first three, according to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, are fully possessed by those in the two lower realms.
These are called the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
First, among the various classes of beings, they arise only in ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Second, because they obstruct the attainment of the lower fruits [of the path], they are also termed lower fetters.
It obstructs only the first fruit.
According to the Abhidharma, those that are merely inferior among the fetters are called "inferior fetters" (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana);
the meaning is the same as the previous explanation.
Those that do not obstruct the lower fruits are called "lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
These three types obstruct the three fruits of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, and Anāgāmin;
the latter two are afflictions belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because they belong to the lower realms, they are called "lower fetters" (avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
One who abides in the fruit of *anāgāmin* severs only these five;
one who advances toward *anāgāmin* also severs the upper fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya*).
Only the final liberation of the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has not yet been realized;
such is the case for the Anāgāmin.
Next, the meaning of Arhat will be explained in detail.
Within this section, there are three gates of analysis:
first, determining its essence;
second, discerning its characteristics.
Regarding the meaning of the number of fetters severed by the three knowledges (*trividyā*):
as for the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), its essence consists of the noble virtues of the fruit of arhatship.
Within the fruit of Arhatship, there are two aspects of noble virtue:
first, the essence of the fruit itself.
According to the Abhidharma, this is analyzed through the cultivation of practice.
Only the final liberation within the nine grades of the antidote for the stage of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception constitutes its resultant essence; within this essence,
it is divided into the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
That which is attained by those of dull faculties is simply called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
That which is attained by those of sharp faculties is called both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Why is this so?
When those of dull faculties attain this knowledge, they are able to exhaust all afflictions; therefore,
it is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (kṣayajñāna).
Because one cannot guarantee that future bonds will not arise,
for this reason it is not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
That which is attained by those of sharp faculties brings about the present exhaustion of all afflictions.
It is also called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Furthermore, because it can ensure that future fetters (*saṃyojana*) will not arise, it is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Question:
Do the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) occur in a single moment, or should they be considered a continuum?
According to that school’s tenet, each occurs in a distinct single moment;
there is no sense of continuity.
Therefore, the treatise states:
"There is not even a single moment of dual thought,
let alone a long succession of them."
Question: If this is called "a single thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa), how can one distinguish the differences between the four types of knowledge?
Explanation:
The meaning of "a single thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa) is explained as being fourfold;
it does not refer to four [moments] occurring sequentially. What is the meaning of this?
The complete exhaustion of causes in a single thought-moment is called "the end of birth";
the fulfillment of the practice of the Path is called "the establishment of the holy life";
and the ultimate realization of cessation is called "that which was to be done has been accomplished."
To permanently abandon future suffering is called "not receiving a subsequent existence.
The distinction in meaning within the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) is likewise so.
Such is the cultivation of practice.
How is it that the cultivation of analytical supernormal powers subsumes all preceding untainted factors to form a single type, the fruit of arhatship?
What is the meaning of this?
At the moment of realizing arhatship, all the untainted acquisitions (*anāsrava-prāpti*) from the causal stage are abandoned simultaneously and instantaneously;
a distinct kind of resultant acquisition arises anew,
whereby one attains the final liberation at the end of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, all the aforementioned untainted [dharmas] combine to constitute a single fruit of arhatship. According to the *Tattvasiddhi*,
it speaks only of cultivation through practice (*pratipatti-bhāvanā*) and does not establish cultivation through acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*).
Therefore, it is taught that only the liberation of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" constitutes the fruit of arhatship.
Within this fruit, regardless of whether one's faculties are sharp or dull,
all possess both the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
In that school’s system, the noble wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) which exhausts the causes of birth and death is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*);
that which enables one never again to undergo future results is called the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpādajñāna*).
The liberation of non-perception possesses these two capacities;
therefore, all beings equally possess both types of wisdom.
These two wisdoms are of one essence, distinguished only according to their respective functions.
The continuity of many thoughts does not cease at a single moment;
such is the nature of the fruit.
Second is the right view of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Exhausting the state of non-arising, one subsequently dwells in the contemplation of the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Such is the essential nature of this meditative concentration; thus concludes this first section.
Next, its characteristics will be distinguished, wherein the opening and closing [of the categories] are not fixed.
In brief, they are of one kind;
or, when divided, there are two:
first, those liberated through wisdom (prajñā-vimukta).
Those liberated in both ways are called "liberated in both respects. Those who have not attained the meditative absorption of cessation are called "liberated by wisdom.
Those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation are called "liberated in both respects."
Furthermore, there are two types:
first, those liberated at any time;
second, those not liberated at any time.
Those with dull faculties of wisdom attain liberation by depending upon time and relying upon a specific place;
this is called "liberation through time" (samayavimukta). Those with sharp faculties attain liberation without depending on time or place.
This is called "liberation at non-specific times" (asamaya-vimukti).
Alternatively, it may be divided into six types,
as explained in the Abhidharma.

First is the one subject to regression, second is the one of reflection, third is the one who guards, fourth is the one who abides, fifth is the one destined for advancement, and sixth is named the immovable.
Regarding the one subject to regression:
originally in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), they lack constant application of skillful means.
One who cannot fall away from what has been attained through sudden means is called a person of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
As for the "one of the nature of reflection" (*cetana-dharman*):
Furthermore, one who possesses both the gradual and sudden two types of skillful means,
and is capable of cultivating the aspiration so that their practice does not regress,
is called a person of the Dharma-characteristic (dharmalakṣaṇa).
Regarding the protection of the Dharma:
there is the constant expedient, but no sudden expedient;
one constantly guards oneself to ensure that practice does not regress.
They are called those who protect the Dharma.
Regarding those who dwell in the Dharma, there are two types of skillful means: the sudden skillful means and the gradual skillful means.
Because the roots of goodness attained neither advance nor retreat,
it is called "abiding.
As for those who must surely ascend:
There are gradual means and sudden means;
one who possesses sudden faculties and is capable of attaining immovability through both means is called "one certain to advance."
Regarding those of immovable dharma:
they possess both gradual means and sudden means;
because that which is attained by these individuals of sharp faculties is firm and stable, it is called "immovable."
Within this, there are two types:
first, immovability that is primordial;
second, immovability attained through progress upon reaching the fruit.
Among these six types, if one speaks of "retrogression," they will certainly regress;
likewise, up to "certain advancement," they will certainly advance upward.
This applies to Arhats of the desire realm, but not to those of the two higher realms.
In those two higher realms, there are only those of stable nature (*sthita-dharman*) and those of immovable nature (*akopya-dharman*).
If one speaks of falling away, it refers to the possibility of falling;
it does not necessarily entail actual falling.
Furthermore, when one who is progressing is able to progress, this is called "progression.
Even if there is regression, such a person, through the application of volition (*cetanā*) and protection, remains in their state;
subsequently, they prevent the loss of their fundamental lineage (*gotra*) and do not allow it to regress or be lost.
As stated above, Arhats of the three realms all possess these six types.
Among the six, the first five are those liberated by occasion (*samaya-vimukta*), while the last one is the one not dependent on occasion (*asamaya-vimukta*).
Alternatively, they may be divided into nine,
as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*,
the first being the sign of regression.
Second is the sign of guarding;
third is the sign of death;
fourth is the sign of progress.
Fifth is the characteristic of abiding;
sixth is the characteristic of non-destruction;
seventh is the characteristic of non-retrogression.
Eighth, liberation through wisdom;
ninth, simultaneous liberation.
The treatise itself explains:
There are distinctions based on the faculties such as faith;
those with the most dull faculties are called "those characterized by regression.
These correspond to the "persons subject to regression" (parihāṇadharman) in the Abhidharma.
However, in the Abhidharma, one falls away from the noble path;
in the Satyasiddhi-śāstra, one falls away from samādhi;
therefore, untainted wisdom cannot manifest before one.
Question: If noble wisdom recedes and does not manifest, how can one attain the fruit of arhatship?
Explanation:
Although he regressed at that time, he later regained it;
having attained it, he gave rise to wisdom and thus became an Arhat.
Regarding what is called "guarding the characteristics," the faculties are slightly superior to those mentioned previously.
In what way are they superior?
Those who are subject to regression will inevitably fall away even if they protect themselves;
as for those who maintain the signs, they regress if they do not guard themselves,
but do not regress if they do guard themselves.
The *Avivartika-samādhi*.
This refers to those who protect the Dharma according to the Abhidharma (*Vibhāṣā*).
Regarding what is called the "sign of death":
The faculties become even more superior than before,
yet one feels such deep revulsion toward all states of existence that one is unable to attain meditative concentration.
Because concentration is not attained, untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) is difficult to manifest.
Because one fears losing what has been obtained and thus seeks to take one's own life,
it is called the "sign of death," as in the case of Ghoṭī and others.
This refers to those who contemplate dharmas according to the Abhidharma.
These three abide in the samādhi of the stage of retrogression (*hāna-bhāgīya*).
As for the phrase "abiding in characteristics":
The samādhi attained neither advances nor recedes;
this refers to one who dwells in the Dharma according to the Abhidharma (Abhidharmika).
Such a person abides in the samādhi of the stage of abiding.
Regarding the "signs of progress":
when the samādhis one has attained become increasingly deep and further enhanced, this is called the sign of progress.
This corresponds to what is termed "necessity for advancement" (*avaśyotkṛṣṭatā*) in the Abhidharma.
This person dwells in the samādhi of progressive increase (*vardhamāna-bhāgīya*). Regarding the "indestructible characteristic" (*akopya-lakṣaṇa*):
the various causes and conditions that might arise cannot destroy the samādhi attained; thus it is called the indestructible characteristic.
Because this person possesses sharp wisdom and skillfully grasps the signs of entering, abiding in, and arising from samādhi,
they are indestructible; such is the characteristic of non-retrogression.
The merit attained by this person is supreme and entirely free from retrogression;
this is called the mark of non-retrogression.
Hereafter, these two persons abide in the stage of certainty (*nyāma*).
Among the Abhidharmikas, those who are immovable are not called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta) because they do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).
Those who do attain the meditative absorption of cessation are called "doubly liberated" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta).
The nine kinds are thus;
when subdivided, they are immeasurable.
Having thus distinguished their characteristics, these two gates are concluded.
Next, the extent to which an arhat has severed the fetters is explained.
In the sūtras it is proclaimed that one becomes an arhat by severing the five higher fetters.
What are the five fetters?
They are: attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
Craving for the realm of form is called "defilement of form";
craving for the formless realm is called "defilement of the formless.
These two are identical to the single defilement of craving within the category of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The latent tendency of ignorance and delusion;
the latent tendencies of conceit and pride—
these are the natures of the aforementioned latent tendencies.
What is called "restlessness and frivolity" (auddhatya-kaukṛtya) refers to the fetter of restlessness (auddhatya-saṃyojana).
These five are the afflictions of the upper realms.

Therefore, it is called the "higher fetter" (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana). Furthermore, that which is produced by an Anāgāmin who has transcended [the desire realm] is also called the higher fetter. Question:
How does this differ from the four floods (*ogha*) and the four yokes (*yoga*) of affliction?
The explanation states:
these five also universally comprise what is subsumed under those floods and yokes.
However, while the outflows (*āsrava*) and the yokes (*yoga*) arise in both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*), these five [fetters] arise only in noble ones,
because they are the fetters that an *anāgāmin* has abandoned.
These five "ends of exhaustion" (kṣayasthāna) are explained as the fruit of arhatship;
therefore, it is said that the arhat abandons the five higher fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana).
Question: [Why is this so?]
For what reason, among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*),
is it specifically said that Arhats have abandoned greed, delusion, and pride, while the others are not mentioned?
This is because the five views and doubt are abandoned during the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Therefore, this is not discussed here.
Hatred exists in the desire realm and is exhausted at the stage of non-returner (anāgāmin).
Therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Question: For what reason are [only some] among the ten envelopments (paryavasthāna) [discussed]?
The reason for specifically mentioning the abandonment of *styāna* (sloth) while not mentioning the others is that,
according to the Abhidharma, among the ten *paryavasthānas* (envelopments),
eight belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because these are exhausted at the stage of the Anāgāmin, they are not mentioned here.
The two envelopments of torpor and restlessness pertain to both of the upper realms;
torpor is thus included among the remaining fetters.
The state of being asleep with respect to all afflictions is called "sleep.
It is not discussed separately because it is explained in accordance with the other fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, sleep is not mentioned because it is conducive to right meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, sleep belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*);
therefore, it is not mentioned here.
Restlessness (auddhatya) is not like the preceding [hindrances];
therefore, it is singled out for mention.
Question: [Why is this?]
The Arhats sever the enveloping fetters (*paryavasthāna*) and thus they are said to have abandoned the "upper fetters.

Why is it that the Anāgāmins— who sever the enveloping fetters such as shamelessness (*ahrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), stinginess (*mātsarya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), anger (*krodha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*),
regret (*kaukṛtya*), and sleep (*middha*)— are not said to have abandoned the "lower fetters"?
The commentary states:
This category should properly be termed the "lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*);
however, the *anāgāmin* has abandoned a greater number of faults.
Since the root differs from the branches, even when speaking of the intermediate state, one speaks of the five lower fetters;
the *paryavasthānas* (obsessions) and *mala*s (stains) are discussed separately. For an Arhat, the faults severed are narrow and few.
Therefore, they are collectively explained as the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) by way of their entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). Question:
As was stated previously...
The Anāgāmin abandons the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).

Among these five lower fetters, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*) have been completely abandoned by the Srotāpanna;
these, taken together from the preceding [stage] up to the subsequent one, constitute the five fetters abandoned by the Anāgāmin.
Now, regarding the Arhat: why is it that,
instead of subsuming the preceding [stages] and combining them with the subsequent to state that ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned,
one speaks only of abandoning five?
The commentary states:
Among those five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), the first three are categorized as being abandoned by the *srotāpanna* when analyzed according to their specific characteristics.
However, when analyzed according to their actual subtlety, there is also the sense that they are directly abandoned by the *anāgāmin*.
Therefore, they are subsumed and combined as the five fetters to be abandoned by the Anāgāmin;
there is no principle that an Arhat directly abandons them.
For this reason, they cannot be subsumed from the latter [category].
It is taught that Arhats sever the ten fetters (saṃyojana).
What is the meaning of this?
Among the five lower fetters, the first three fetters are directly severed in three locations.
The first person, by gradually severing the three fetters, becomes a *srotāpanna*.
The second person, by transcending [the stages] and directly severing the three fetters, becomes a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
When this person was an ordinary being, they severed the fetters of desire up to the exhaustion of the sixth grade.
Subsequently, upon entering the path of seeing and severing the three fetters,
at the moment of the sixteenth mental state— the subsequent knowledge of the path— they become a sakṛdāgāmin.
Therefore, the Sūtra proclaims:
"The Sakṛdāgāmin person has severed the three fetters and attenuated greed, hatred, and delusion.
The third, the Anāgāmin who has transcended, has personally severed the three fetters and become an Anāgāmin."
When this person was an ordinary being, they had severed the fetters of desire up to the exhaustion of the ninth grade.
Subsequently, upon entering the path of seeing and severing the three fetters,
at the moment of the sixteenth cognition of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), they immediately become a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Because this principle exists, it is said in the sūtras that an anāgāmin severs the five lower fetters;
however, there is no case where one who has completely severed the five lower fetters immediately becomes an arhat.
Therefore, it is not said that an Arhat severs the ten fetters.
Such is the case for an Arhat;
this is a brief summary of the noble ones among the Śrāvakas.
Next, the Pratyekabuddhas are discussed.
Within this, there are three sub-sections for analysis.
First, the explanation of the name and its meaning.
Second, the detailed analysis in relation to the small;
third, the detailed analysis in relation to the great.
First, the explanation of the names and meanings.
Regarding the term "Pratyekabuddha," its correct foreign pronunciation is *Pizhifo* (Pratyekabuddha).
Here, *pratyeka* is translated as "dependent origination" (*yinyuan*),
and *buddha* is translated as "awakened" (*jue*).
There are two ways to explain the meaning of the term *pratyekabuddha*.
First, it is explained by way of the dharma-gate that is observed:
"pratyaya" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).
Observing [the process] from ignorance up to old age and death, one attains awakening through these conditions;
therefore, they are called Pratyekabuddhas (Solitary Realizers).
Second, this is explained by way of the causes and conditions for attaining the Way.
This is as explained in detail in the *Pratyekabuddhamārgopāya-sūtra*:
for example, like Vakkali,
who attained awakening when the wind stirred the trees.
All such as these attain awakening by relying on the conditions of present events;
therefore, they are called *Pratyekabuddhas* (Solitary Realizers). Such is the definition and meaning of this term; this section concludes.
Next is the detailed analysis of the minor [categories].
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the identification of the characteristics of the minor [categories].
Second, the clarification of similarities and differences.
Regarding the "discernment of characteristics," the Sūtra explains that there are two gates for distinguishing between Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
First, they are distinguished according to the dharma-gates that serve as their objects of contemplation.
Those who attain the Way by contemplating the Four Noble Truths are all termed Śrāvakas;
those who attain the Way by contemplating the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are collectively called Pratyekabuddhas.

If, according to this principle, those who encounter a Buddha in the present time and attain the Way through his teaching of the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are likewise included among the Pratyekabuddhas;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
For the sake of instructing the śrāvakas, he taught the Four Noble Truths;
for the sake of instructing the pratyekabuddhas, he taught the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Within these pratyekabuddhas, there is a further subdivision into two types.
First, the pratyekabuddha-pratyekabuddha:
this person originally seeks the path of the pratyekabuddha;
they constantly delight in observing the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, thereby perfecting the nature of a pratyekabuddha.
In their final body, they do not encounter the era of a Buddha;
yet, by relying on the conditions of present events, they attain awakening to the Way.
Because their original nature as a pratyekabuddha is now awakened by means of these situational conditions.
They are taught as pratyekabuddhas because they are pratyekabuddhas.
There are two types of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
these people originally sought the path of a pratyekabuddha.
They also delight in contemplating the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination to fulfill the nature of a pratyekabuddha;
in their final body, they encounter a Buddha who explains the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination for them, whereby they attain awakening and understanding.
Because they attain awakening by hearing from the Buddha,
they are called Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;
Mahākāśyapa is such a person.
What is stated in the sūtras as being taught for the sake of the pratyekabuddhas refers precisely to this.
This is also termed "pratyekabuddha-śrāvaka";
therefore, it was analyzed among the śrāvakas above.
The former category distinguishes them based on their dharma;
the second distinguishes them based on the causes and conditions for attaining the Way.
Those who attain the Way by hearing sounds from others are all termed śrāvakas.
Therefore, although those such as Mahākāśyapa attained awakening by contemplating the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination,
they did so because they gained understanding by hearing it from the Buddha.
In the sutras, they are described as the assembly of śrāvakas.
Those who attain the Way by relying on present conditions are collectively termed pratyekabuddhas.
According to this meaning, even those srotāpannas who are to undergo seven more births may not encounter the era of a Buddha in their final existence.
Those who attain the Way by relying on present conditions are also subsumed under the category of *pratyekabuddhas*.
Within these *pratyekabuddhas*, there is a further subdivision into two types:
first, the *pratyekabuddha-pratyekabuddha*.
The meaning is as explained above.
Second, regarding the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:
these individuals have originally sought the path of the śrāvaka.
By contemplating the Four Noble Truths, one realizes the path and attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Because one's faculties are dull, one does not attain *nirvāṇa* in the present life;
rather, one undergoes rebirth seven times among gods and humans.
In their final body, they do not encounter the era of a Buddha;
rather, they attain the state of a pratyekabuddha by relying on present circumstances and conditions. Therefore, they are called pratyekabuddhas.
For this reason, they are termed śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
These are also called pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas;
therefore, they were distinguished among the aforementioned śrāvakas.
Herein, one should apply a fourfold logical analysis (catuṣkoṭi).
First, there are those who are śrāvakas but not pratyekabuddhas.
As for what is called a "śrāvaka," this refers to a person who is a śrāvaka;
the meaning of this is as explained above.
The second is one who is a pratyekabuddha rather than a śrāvaka.
This refers to a person who is a pratyekabuddha;
this is also explained as above.
Third are those who are both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
namely, those srotāpannas who will be reborn seven more times and,
in their final body, attain awakening alone because they do not encounter a Buddha in the world.
The fourth are pratyekabuddhas, who are also śrāvakas;
these are those in their final existence who encounter a Buddha and, upon hearing him teach the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, attain realization.
Such is the analysis of their characteristics.
Next, the discussion turns to similarities and differences.
Among the first four types of persons, we shall first distinguish their similarities and differences based on the first fruit of realization.
First, the discussion of commonality.
There are five kinds of commonality:
first, commonality in the realization of principle.
Because they perceive the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas perceive that within the aggregates (*skandha*) and apart from the aggregates, a self (*ātman*) cannot be found."
Both the aggregates (*skandhas*) and that which is apart from the aggregates lack a self or a human nature;
in both cases, the obstacles are severed equally.
Equally, they sever the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*) and do not undergo further分段 (*bheda-bhāga*, i.e., fragmented rebirth).
As stated in the Śrīmālā-sūtra,
the three types of practice are identical,
for they equally cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Their path is the same as that of the śrāvakas;
the four attainments of the fruits are the same."
Because they equally attain the fruits of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"One who, in their final body, attains the fruit of arhatship through self-awakening without a teacher is called a pratyekabuddha."
The five types of realization of cessation are identical in that they equally realize both *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) nirvāṇa; however,
regarding these five, there are not a few subtle differences when discussed in detail.
Generally speaking, in broad outline, all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and human beings are entirely the same.
Next, regarding the points of difference, there are six kinds.
The first is the difference in faculties (indriya).
The śrāvaka has dull faculties, while the pratyekabuddha has sharp faculties.
A question is asked:
"The pratyekabuddha’s vision of reality is the same as that of the śrāvaka."
What is meant by "sharp faculties"?
The explanation states:
although their vision of principle is the same as that of the śrāvakas, it is called "sharp" because it is clear, pure, and swift.
Furthermore, although their severance of afflictions is equally swift through diligence as that of the śrāvakas,
they are also called "beneficial" because they do not regress;
secondly, their basis is different.
Śrāvakas rely on a teacher, while pratyekabuddhas do not;
this is the third difference regarding their conditions.
Śrāvakas attain realization of the Path by relying on the teachings as their condition.
Pratyekabuddhas attain awakening and understanding by relying on the manifest conditions of phenomenal characteristics.
Fourth, there is a difference in their objects of observation: Śrāvakas observe the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
The Pratyekabuddhas contemplate the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination.
It is asked:
What did Śrīmālā proclaim?
When those of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha vehicles first contemplate the Noble Truths,
that text further states:
"The World-Honored One shall provide for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas the teaching of the four reliances."
Regarding the "four reliances," they refer to the four noble truths.
If this is so, then Pratyekabuddhas also contemplate the Four Noble Truths;
why, then, is it said that Pratyekabuddhas specifically contemplate the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination? To explain:
Although Pratyekabuddhas contemplate causes and conditions, they also separately perform the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths based on those causes and conditions.
Therefore, the Sūtras speak of them as "contemplating the truths.
What is the meaning of this?

Prior to the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan), one performs the analytical contemplation (*vibhaṅga-smṛtyupasthāna*) by separately observing the twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time;

subsequently, one performs the comprehensive contemplation (*saṃbheda-smṛtyupasthāna*) by observing the suffering, impermanence, and other characteristics of these twelve links of dependent origination.

From the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summit (mūrdhan) upward, one performs the contemplation of the forty-four knowledges (*jñāna*) based upon the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
This is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) and "contemplation of the truths" (*satyavipaśyanā*). What are these forty-four knowledges?
The twelve links of dependent origination, through their mutual connection of cause and effect, consist of twelve pairs. First,
taking the subsequent pairs as the basis, one contemplates them as the Four Noble Truths, as follows:
Old age and death, the origin of old age and death, the cessation of old age and death, and the path leading to the cessation of old age and death.
The first is the contemplation of suffering;
the second is the contemplation of the origin.
The third is the contemplation of cessation;
the fourth is the contemplation of the path.
Thus, by tracing back in reverse order, each of the initial pairs consists of these four contemplations.
Therefore, taken together, there are forty-four.
For this reason, the pratyekabuddha is named "one who contemplates the truths" (*satyadarśin*). Question:
The Sūtra states:

"Because the twelve links of dependent origination are contemplated with inferior wisdom, one attains the enlightenment of a śrāvaka; because they are contemplated with middling wisdom, [one attains the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha]."
From the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas up to the supreme, unsurpassed *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
even śrāvakas contemplate dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
How can it then be said that śrāvakas exclusively contemplate the Four Noble Truths?
The commentary states:
Although the śrāvakas contemplate the four truths, the suffering and its origin among them are precisely the twelvefold law of dependent origination (dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda) of birth and death.
Therefore, it is also called the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
Such is the general characteristic.
Within this, the śrāvaka’s correct contemplation of the dharma-gate of the four noble truths is distinguished.
The Pratyekabuddha correctly contemplates the gateway of the twelve links of dependent origination;
this is the fourth difference. Fifth, there is a difference regarding the orientation toward the fruit.
Among śrāvakas, there are the four stages of approach and the four fruits;
among pratyekabuddhas, there is only one stage of approach and one fruit. Why is this so?
The śrāvaka has dull faculties;
he cannot observe the continuity [of the mind] to its ultimate conclusion in a single moment,
but repeatedly emerges from his exertion and takes rest.
Therefore, many fruits are distinguished;
because the fruits are numerous, the paths leading toward them are also distinct.
Pratyekabuddhas possess sharp faculties.
Once one enters the contemplation of the noble ones, it proceeds in uninterrupted succession until its ultimate consummation;
because there is no point of cessation midway, there are not multiple fruits.
Because there are not multiple fruits, multiple paths (nirvedhabhāgīya) are not established.
However, within a single contemplation of the continuum,
that which is incomplete is judged to be "one-sided," while that which is complete is said to be "a single fruit."
Therefore, the *Gṛhapati-sūtra* speaks of ten noble natures (*ārya-gotra*):
for śrāvakas there are mostly eight,
while for pratyekabuddhas two are established.
Sixth is the difference in the range of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, the range of the Śrāvaka’s supernormal power extends over two thousand lands.
The Pratyekabuddhas have three thousand world-systems as their common sphere of activity.
Furthermore, as stated in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra,
among the Śrāvakas, those who do not apply focused attention [possess this range].
A thousand lands constitute the range of his physical vision;
two thousand lands constitute the range of his mental attention. Among the great śrāvakas, those who do not apply such mental attention [have a range of one thousand lands].
Two thousand lands constitute the range of his communication.
As for his mental application (*manasikāra*), three thousand lands constitute the range of his communication.
Among those who are *pratyekabuddhas*, there are both great and small.
For a person of the stage of a minor pratyekabuddha who does not apply mental attention,
two thousand world-systems constitute the range of their communication;
for one who applies mental attention, three thousand world-systems constitute the range of their communication.
As for the Great Pratyekabuddhas, one need not inquire whether they are engaged in mental attention or non-attention;
all take the trichiliocosm as their sphere of supernormal power.
These are called the differences in the scope of their supernormal powers.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*,
if a śrāvaka wishes to know the initial mind [of a stream-enterer], they will only come to know it upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind;
whereas a pratyekabuddha who wishes to know that initial mind will know it immediately upon reaching the sixth moment of mind.
This, too, is a distinction within the general [category]. Question:
For what reason is it that one must know from the first moment of mind until the sixth moment of mind before one finally knows?
The Pratyekabuddha, intending to know the mind of the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*, concentrates his mind and observes it.
Once that *kṣānti* has passed away, he enters the *duḥkhe-dharma-jñāna* and immediately thereafter contemplates it.

Once that knowledge has ceased, one enters the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding suffering by taking the suffering of the higher realms as its object;
the awakening then investigates the tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) within the desire realm itself.
He abandons the superior suffering and the origin [of suffering] pertaining to the desire realm.
At the time of patience (*kṣānti*), one has not yet known [the truth]; it is only upon reaching the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*) that one first knows it.
For this reason, it is said that the sixth mind is known.
The similarities and differences between the first two types of persons are thus.
Next, the third type will be examined in contrast to the preceding two to distinguish their similarities and differences.
Among those who have attained *srotāpanna*, there are those who undergo rebirth seven times at most.
Regarding those who, in their final body, do not encounter a Buddha but become pratyekabuddhas:
compared to the aforementioned śrāvakas, they share nine similarities and have two differences.
As for the nine similarities:
First, the identity of the realization of principle;
second, the identity of the severance of hindrances;
third, the identity of cultivation.
Fourth, they are identical in attaining the fruits;
fifth, they are identical in realizing cessation;
sixth, they are identical in their faculty-natures.
Seventh, the contemplation of phenomena is the same.
Eighth, the orientation toward the fruit is the same.
Ninth, the universal application is the same.
All is as explained above.
Regarding the two differences:
first, the difference in their bases.
In their final body, they do not rely on a teacher;
secondly, they differ in terms of conditions,
as they attain the fruit without depending on verbal instruction.
Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas who look toward their former conditions, there are seven similarities and four differences between them and [the Śrāvakas].
As for the seven similarities: first, they are identical in their realization of the principle (dharma).
Second, they are identical in the severance of hindrances;
third, they are identical in their practice;
fourth, they are identical in the attainment of the fruit.
5. The proof of cessation is the same;
it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
6. The basis is the same.
In their final existence, they do not rely on the instructions of a teacher;
seventh, they share the same conditions,
for they attain the Way by relying equally upon causal circumstances.
Regarding the four differences:
first is the difference in faculties;
this person has dull faculties.
Second, the difference in the contemplation of dharmas:
this awakening [contemplates] the Four Truths.
Third, the difference in the orientation toward the fruit.
This person is fully endowed with the four paths and four fruits;
while the four [paths and fruits] differ in their specific functions, this person’s [attainment] is comprehensive yet inferior.
Next, one shall distinguish the similarities and differences between the fourth [category] and the first two persons.
Regarding those who, in their final body, encounter a Buddha who preaches the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination and thereby attain awakening:
Regarding the similarities and differences between the Śrāvakas before the full moon and the Śrāvakas themselves, there are seven points of similarity and four points of difference.
As for the seven similarities, the first is the identity in their realization of the principle (*tattva*).
Second, they are identical in the severance of hindrances;
third, they are identical in their practice;
fourth, they are identical in the attainment of the fruit.
Fifth, the equality of the realization of cessation is entirely as distinguished above.
Sixth, the equality of the basis.
One attains deliverance by relying on a teacher;
seventh, they share the same conditions,
for both equally rely upon the verbal teachings.
Regarding the four differences:
first, the difference in the nature of the faculties;
this person possesses sharp faculties.
Second, the difference in the awakening to phenomena;
third, the difference in the conditions for this awakening; fourth, the difference in the orientation toward the fruit.
This [attainment] does not distinguish between the four fruits and the four paths; while the four [paths and fruits] differ in their general application,
this person’s application is superior.
Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas, there are nine points of similarity and two points of difference between them and the [śrāvakas].
As for the nine similarities:
first, the similarity in their realization of the principle.
Second, they are identical in the abandonment of hindrances;
third, they are identical in their practice;
fourth, they are identical in the attainment of the fruit.
Fifth, the realization of cessation is the same;
sixth, the nature of the faculties is the same;
seventh, the observation of dharmas is the same.
The eight [paths] toward the fruits are identical;
each one is directed toward a single fruit.
The nine [fruits] are generally identical in their application.
All is as explained above.
Regarding the two differences,
the first is the difference in their basis (*āśraya*).
This person relies upon a teacher;
secondly, they differ in terms of the conditions they rely upon,
for this one relies upon verbal instruction.
The explanation of these two gateways regarding the Small [Vehicle] is thus concluded.
Next, they are distinguished with respect to the Great [Vehicle].
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the differentiation of characteristics;
second, the clarification of similarities and differences.
Regarding the "differentiation of characteristics":
There are two types of pratyekabuddhas.
One is the pratyekabuddha of the lineage;
such a person has originally practiced the path of a pratyekabuddha and thus established the nature of a pratyekabuddha.
In their final body, they contemplate the law of dependent origination and realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha.
Second are the regressive pratyekabuddhas;
these individuals previously practiced the Mahāyāna in the past.
If one retreats and dwells in the middle [vehicle], it can likewise be divided into three types.
The first two are as described above;
to these, one further adds the type of *nirmāṇa-pratyekabuddha*.
This means that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest themselves for this purpose;
thus the heavenly maiden said:
Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of causes and conditions, I am a pratyekabuddha.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also says:
"Knowing that the multitude delights in the small and fears great wisdom."
Therefore, bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas,
pratyekabuddhas, and so forth.
Such are their distinct characteristics.
Next, we shall distinguish their similarities and differences in relation to the Mahāyāna.
Regarding their similarities:
those pratyekabuddhas, having once entered the noble path, never again fall back.
This is the same as for Bodhisattvas.
It is not like Śrāvakas who, having attained the state of an Ārya, may fall back.
For what reason do Pratyekabuddhas never fall back?
Because they possess sharp faculties, they exclusively employ the untainted (*anāsrava*) path to sever the fetters of outflows (*āsravasaṃyojana*).
This is truly because their non-retrogression is identical to that of the bodhisattvas.
Thus, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that pratyekabuddhas and bodhisattvas together constitute "mature ghee" (*pakvasarpis*).
Regarding what is called "difference," there are briefly ten types.
The first is difference of cause.
That pratyekabuddha takes as his basis the narrow and inferior roots of goodness cultivated in the past;
because he does not extensively transform sentient beings, it is called "narrow," and because he does not seek the wisdom of a Buddha, it is described as "inferior."
First, they do not know that the causal practices of a bodhisattva are vast and great.
Second, their faculties differ:
the pratyekabuddha has dull faculties.
The Bodhisattva possesses sharp faculties;
because the understanding of the Pratyekabuddha is narrow and shallow, it is not swift,
and is therefore termed "dull."
The understanding of a bodhisattva is profound, vast, steep, and swift;
therefore, it is called "sharp.
Third, their minds differ.
The Pratyekabuddha fears suffering and seeks its cessation with haste;
the Bodhisattva does not fear it and constantly delights in remaining in the world.
Thus, there are four differences in their respective understandings.
Pratyekabuddhas realize the emptiness of persons by contemplating only the twelve links of dependent origination;
Bodhisattvas universally contemplate all phenomena and fully understand both types of emptiness.
Thus, there are five differences in their modes of practice.
Pratyekabuddhas cultivate only the path of self-benefit,
whereas Bodhisattvas benefit both themselves and others.
Furthermore, Bodhisattvas practice the six perfections.
Pratyekabuddhas do not cultivate this.
There is a difference regarding the abandonment of obstacles:
pratyekabuddhas are only able to abandon the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
For a bodhisattva, the two obstacles are eliminated simultaneously.
The meaning of these two obstacles has been explained extensively above.
Seventh, there is a difference in the attainment of the fruit.
The Pratyekabuddha correctly attains the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
the Bodhisattva is able to skillfully possess Great Parinirvāṇa.
The meanings of "small" and "great" Nirvāṇa will be explained later.
Eighth, the difference in the arising of emanations,
as explained in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
the pratyekabuddhas who emanate beings manifest only supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Throughout the entire day, he remains silent and says nothing;
the bodhisattva is not like this,
for he is able to manifest and to speak.
For what reason are Pratyekabuddhas unable to preach the Dharma?
When Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world, there are no ninefold scriptures;
thus, there is nothing to be proclaimed.
Furthermore, because Pratyekabuddhas lack the skillful means of compassion, they are unable to teach.
Lacking compassion, they do not give rise to the intention to speak.
Because they lack the wisdom of the unimpeded skillful means of the four immeasurables, they are incapable of teaching.
Ninth, they differ in their common application,
as explained in detail in the section on the meaning of the latter six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Tenth, they differ in their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
All the physical, intellectual, and meritorious qualities of the pratyekabuddhas are impermanent, suffering, non-self, and impure;
the true virtues of the bodhisattvas, however, are permanent, blissful, self, and pure.
Furthermore, the nirvāṇa attained by pratyekabuddhas possesses only bliss and purity, but lacks self and permanence.
The nirvāṇa of a bodhisattva is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
these ten aspects also differ from those of the śrāvaka.
However, for now, let us explain them with reference to the pratyekabuddha.
The Pratyekabuddhas are likewise.
Next, regarding the Bodhisattva, there are three sections for analysis within this [treatise].
First, the explanation of the meaning of the name.
Second, the analysis by way of pairs;
third, the analysis by way of specific characteristics.
First, the explanation of the etymological meaning.
The name "Bodhisattva" is a foreign term.
Its correct name in that foreign land is *bodhisattva*.
Those who transmit it here [in China] render it as "Púxídì."
"Sa" (薩) is abbreviated as "lue" (略), and "tuo" (埵) is "da" (埵); thus, it is called "bodhisattva.
"Bodhi" is translated here as "dao" (道, the path).
"Sattva" is translated here as "sentient being" (zhòngshēng).
This is because such a person seeks the Way within their own mind and is fully endowed with the practice of the Way;
since they have attained the name of a person through the Way, they are called a "Way-being" (dào zhòngshēng).
Question: Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and other such persons all seek the Way;
they all possess the practice of the Way and likewise achieve it through the Way. Why is this so?
For what reason is he not called a bodhisattva,
while this person alone is designated as a bodhisattva?
To explain:
The names "Worthy" (ārya) and "Sage" (muni) possess both universal and restricted applications.
When applied universally, their meanings are equivalent;
thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
Even those as far as the *srotāpanna* are called *bodhisattvas* and may also be designated as Buddhas;
because they seek the path of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they are called *bodhisattvas*.
Because he possesses both the common and uncommon paths of perfect enlightenment, he is called a Buddha.
However, because the sūtras wish to distinguish between the noble ones and the ordinary,
they specifically designate those of the Great Vehicle as bodhisattvas.
Since [the qualities] are shared equally among the noble ones (ārya),
for what reason is this specifically designated as "bodhisattva"?
There are three reasons for this distinction.
First, explaining this in terms of the aspirational mind (*praṇidhāna-citta*) in expectation of the fruit:
only these sentient beings seek great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), while all others do not;
therefore, they alone are called "beings on the path" (*mārga-sattva*).
Therefore, the *Dichilun* states:
"The first is the one who has made a definitive vow for great bodhi; this refers specifically to the bodhisattva.
This is explained by looking at the aspirational mind in relation to its fruit.
Second, according to the perspective of the mind that understands, one explains it in terms of realization:
ordinary beings abide in existence,
while those of the two vehicles cling to non-existence.
Existence and non-existence diverge from the center and do not accord with the Middle Way;
only the Bodhisattva’s wondrous relinquishing of existence and non-existence accords with the Middle Way.
Therefore, only this is called the Path for sentient beings.
Third is the explanation according to practice.
Within the entry into the Buddha-dharma, there are three gates:
first, the teaching; second, the meaning; and third, practice.
The teaching is shallow while the meaning is profound; conduct is supreme.
Śrāvakas are named according to their dull faculties because they follow the teaching;
"śabda" (sound) refers to the teaching.
One who awakens to understanding through the sound of others' eating is called a Śrāvaka (Hearer).
The Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer) is superior to him; his designation is established based on the meaning [of his realization].
They are called Pratyekabuddhas.
"Pratyaya" means "condition.
They attain awakening through conditions.
Therefore, they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
As for Bodhisattvas, their name is manifested through their supreme practice;
because they are able to accomplish the path that benefits both self and others as well as the benefit of both together, they are called Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
"Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas can only deliver themselves;
bodhisattvas are not like this."
To deliver oneself and to deliver others is called "victory through the Way" (*mārga-vijaya*).
Because of this victory through the Way, they are called "beings of the Way" (*mārga-sattva*).
Such is the meaning of the name; this concludes this section.
Next, regarding the minor distinctions:
there are two types of bodhisattvas;
the first is those who enter gradually.
The second is sudden enlightenment.
As for what is called "gradual entry," it means starting with the small and subsequently proceeding to the great.
A question is asked:
At what time does this person enter the Great [Vehicle]?
The Śākya [Master] replied:
"Within the Small [Vehicle], there are two types of persons."
First, those who are ignorant of the Dharma;
second, those who are not ignorant of the Dharma.
Those who cling to the small and are deluded regarding the great are called "ignorant of the Dharma."
One who knows the small and understands the great is called a person of non-deluded dharma.
Having originally practiced the nature of the small and small,
they encounter a Buddha in their final body and desire the small.
The Buddha taught them based on this so that they might realize the small fruits;
having attained these, they became attached to them and were unable to enter the Great Vehicle.
After their future parinirvāṇa without remainder—
Only when the thought of awakening arises can one turn toward the Great [Vehicle].
The duration of the kalpas is so vast as to be incalculable.
Those who are not deluded regarding the Dharma have already generated the great resolve in past lives.
Wandering through birth and death, they have forgotten their original resolve and momentarily desire the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna).
The Buddha, relying on them, teaches for the sake of attaining the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
Having attained these small fruits, they realize for themselves that there is more to be accomplished and thus resolve their minds toward the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna).
They are able to enter it even in the present life.
It is asked:
Since these individuals have already entered the Mahāyāna, why is this?
Regarding the stage within the Mahāyāna,
there is no definitive determination in the sūtras;
one must infer it solely by its meaning, which suggests it should be situated among the happy destinies (sugati).

Within the Mahāyāna, those who have first resolved their minds [for awakening] but have not yet reached the stage of spiritual lineage (*gotra*) are all termed "those in a fortunate rebirth" (*sugati*).
Since followers of the two vehicles enter the Great Vehicle while in this very stage,
how can it be known that they were not already in a fortunate rebirth prior to this?
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that those prior to attaining the good realms are called "perpetually submerged.

This refers to being perpetually submerged in the three miserable destinies (*tridurgati*) and perpetually submerged within the three realms of existence (*tribhava*); this is not what is meant by "perpetual submersion" here.
Therefore, we know it is not the former.
How is it known that it is not included within the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) following a fortunate rebirth (*sugati*)?
The *Bhūmivastu* proclaims:
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) of a bodhisattva of the lineage (*gotra*) are preeminent and have been so by the very nature of phenomena since beginningless time.
Since this person has not yet manifested the fundamental dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) to constitute these six sense bases,
it is known that they are not yet above the stage of the lineage.
Furthermore, it is said that one who has accomplished the lineage possesses the truly pure dharmas;
yet this person has not yet accomplished them.
It is also said that the nature of the six perfections is accomplished through the lineage.
This person has not yet attained it.
Furthermore, it is said that the lineage (gotra) consists of all the seeds of the Buddha-dharmas within one's body;
this person has not yet fulfilled them. Moreover, it is said that the lineage is the purification of the two obstacles.
This person is only able to purify the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*);
a bodhisattva of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is capable of serving as a refuge for sentient beings,
whereas this person is not yet so capable.
Furthermore, it is said that those of the spiritual lineage (gotra) attain self-awakening through whatever Dharma they hear, rather than awakening through another;
yet this person [in question] relies upon another.
From this, it is known [that he does not possess the lineage].
Those who are not of the [noble] lineage exist only within the happy realms.
It is asked:
since these beings already reside in the happy realms, [why is this so?]
Regarding which of the two types of death they undergo:
the commentary states that this applies from the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the *anāgāmin*.
They undergo death by fragmentation;
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas undergo death by transformation,
as stated in the Śrīmālā-sūtra.
Question: The Śrīmālādevī-sūtra states that bodhisattvas of the highest lineage and great power undergo the death of transformation (pariṇāmikī-maraṇa).
Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas undergo the death of transformation (pariṇāmi-maraṇa),
which is identical to that of those with great power (mahābala).
For what reason, then, is it not determined that this applies to those above the stage of spiritual lineage (gotra)?
The commentary states:
Although the transformation bodies received by these persons are identical to those of the Greatly Powerful One, their meanings differ in many respects;
therefore, they do not constitute the [true] lineage (gotra).
Question: Those of the two vehicles who resolve their minds to seek the Great [Vehicle] are called bodhisattvas.
Such bodhisattvas, while within the happy destinies, receive a body of transformation.

In the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, why is it that only bodhisattvas of great power who have already attained the lineage (*gotra*) and above are said to undergo transformation-death (*pariṇāmikī-cyuti*), while those in the happy realms (*sugati*) undergoing transformation-death are not mentioned?
The explanation states:
There are two gates for explaining the "great":
first, the gate of differentiation,
which differentiates the great from the various smalls.
Only Bodhisattvas of great power within the spiritual lineage (gotra) receive the body of transformation (nirmāṇakāya);
from this point onward, all preceding stages are termed "segmented" (bheda).
Although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas may have resolved upon the Great Mind, they have not yet attained the Great Practice.
It is still explained according to its original name and is not called the "bodhisattva undergoing transformation.
Second is the gate of subsuming characteristics,
which subsumes the small and completes the great.
Among those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, anyone who gives rise to the great resolve is called a bodhisattva.
According to this principle, even those in the state of the good destinies undergo transformation and rebirth.
It is not that those above the stage of "lineage" (gotra) alone undergo it;
rather, what was spoken by Śrīmālā concerning the "powerful ones" (mahābala) refers only to the characteristics of the death of transformation (nirmāṇa-cyuti) for those above that stage.
This is said in contrast to the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Question: Since those of the two vehicles who resolve their minds toward the Great Vehicle are already in the happy realms,
within these happy realms, are they at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end?
The commentary states:
This person is not the same as an ordinary being at the very lowest level;
yet one who has merely first resolved their mind [on awakening] cannot yet be called "superior among those in the happy realms."
How is this known? As it is said in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:
"A person who has attained the stage of *srotāpanna* reaches [nirvāṇa] after eighty thousand kalpas."
The Sakṛdāgāmin arrives after sixty thousand kalpas;
the Anāgāmin arrives after forty thousand kalpas;
and the Arhat arrives after twenty thousand kalpas.
The pratyekabuddha reaches [this stage] after ten thousand kalpas.
When the Sūtra says "reaches," it means reaching the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
this should be designated as the "stage of the lineage" (*gotra-bhūmi*) mind.
This is considered the bodhicitta that has reached its destination;
it is separated from the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotrabhūmi) by such a number of kalpas.
Knowing this,
[one realizes] it is not the highest among the happy realms. He asks:
From all those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* up to those on the path toward *pratyekabuddhahood* within the lineage-ground (*gotrabhūmi*),
their duration ranges from eighty thousand *kalpas* down to ten thousand *kalpas*, with some not reaching even that.
Śāriputra explained:
Those who are not deluded regarding the Dharma now resolve upon the Great Mind and practice the Mahāyāna;
such persons may reach the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) within the span of these kalpas.
However, those deluded persons who grasp at the extinction of the Lesser Vehicle are beyond calculation.
For as many eons as there are atoms, they remain within nirvāṇa.
Once this period has passed, mental conceptions arise once more.
When these mental conceptions have arisen, they resolve their minds toward the Great [Vehicle].
After this, Arhats must further practice and study the Mahāyāna for twenty thousand kalpas before they reach the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra).
Pratyekabuddhas must further practice and study the Mahāyāna for ten thousand kalpas before they reach the stage of the spiritual lineage.
For this reason, it is not the case that all people [remain for] eighty thousand kalpas. Question:
[How can one attain] the fruit of Arhatship after being reborn seven times among humans and in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Sudhāvāsa)?
Since those who undergo rebirth seven times do not exceed one kalpa,
for what reason is there such a vast difference toward the Great [Vehicle]?
Alternatively, it may be granted that the Noble One provisionally acts as a transitional stage.
Furthermore, it is explained:
if a Srotāpanna and so forth advance to sever the remaining fetters and reach the fruit of Arhatship.
Thereafter, those who have turned toward the Great Vehicle do not receive much more;
yet, if they do not further sever their fetters, those who have turned toward the Great Vehicle will possess this degree of distinction.
All remaining fetters are capable of obstructing all the practices and virtues of the Dharma-realm.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are difficult to accomplish, one enters them gradually in this manner.
As for those who speak of "sudden enlightenment," they do not enter from the small [vehicle] and only in a single lifetime study the Great [Vehicle].
A question is asked:
This person has not entered [the path] from the beginning.
What kind of practice must they cultivate to be able to remedy their karmic obstructions and gain entry into the Mahāyāna?
As it is said in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
This refers to the cultivation of the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom.
By cultivating these, one is able to transform karmic obstacles and enter the Mahāyāna.
There are eight sections explaining the body, precepts, mind, and wisdom.
This has been explained in detail above. Question:
What kind of mind must this person generate to be said to have entered the Mahāyāna?
One gives rise to three kinds of minds.
First, the mind that is weary of the conditioned:
upon hearing the teaching that birth and death are impermanent and great suffering, one develops a deep sense of weary detachment.
Second is the mind seeking the unconditioned:
upon hearing the teaching that *nirvāṇa* is eternal, blissful, self, and pure, one makes a deep-seated aspiration and seeks it.
Third is the mind mindful of sentient beings.
Because all sentient beings possess suffering and lack happiness, one resolves to rescue and deliver them.
It is asked:
What kind of practice must this person cultivate to be called a learner of the Mahāyāna?
One cultivates three kinds of practices:
first, the practice of detachment from the conditioned,
which consists of cultivating true contemplation to break through and leave behind birth and death.
Second is the practice of proceeding toward the unconditioned,
which consists of cultivating the six perfections to proceed toward great parinirvāṇa.
Third is the practice of delivering sentient beings.
One practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth to benefit all beings.
It is asked:
Both those who progress gradually and those who attain sudden realization abide in the happy realms (*sugati*).
What is superior? The explanation says:
it is not fixed.
Those who enter from the beginning [the Śrāvaka vehicle] take delight in the practice of existence;
because of their prior habituation, the other two [vehicles] are not as effective for them.
This is because it is difficult to achieve a vast and great mind when one has previously trained in the limited.
For those who attain sudden enlightenment, there are two superior types of practice for seeking birth through the Buddha’s transformation:
they focus their minds on seeking the Buddha in order to deliver sentient beings,
and they loathe existence as being inferior.
Because they constantly aspire to teach and transform sentient beings while remaining within existence, rather than being solely weary of it,
these persons abide in the happy realms and undergo birth through fragmentation (*pariccheda-jāti*) without yet having undergone transformation (*pariṇāmi-jāti*).
Question: Since these [beings] within the happy realms possess mutual degrees of superiority and inferiority,
in what respect can they be considered equal?
That is to say:
it is because upon the spiritual lineage (gotra), all practices must be collectively perfected before one can become a Buddha, as this constitutes the definitive lineage.
The two gates concerning the Hīnayāna are thus concluded.
Next, regarding the Mahāyāna, one should proceed to analyze them according to their specific characteristics.
Within this, first comes the general analysis of their common characteristics.
This will be discussed separately later.
Within the general classification, it is analyzed through various combinations and variations in number;
alternatively, all may be consolidated into one.
That is to say:
among the three vehicles, there is one assembly of bodhisattvas,
which may be divided into two.
The second [category] has two gates:
first, the determinate and the indeterminate;
second, the analysis by way of these two gates.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
Bodhisattvas in the stage of "good destiny" (*sugati*) who repeatedly regress and repeatedly advance are termed "indeterminate" (*aniyata*);
those from the stage of "lineage" (*gotra*) upward, whose progress is firm and superior, are termed "determinate" (*niyata*).
The distinction between the mundane and the supramundane is made in two ways.
That which precedes the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) is called mundane;
that from the first bhūmi upward is called supramundane.
Furthermore, the stages prior to the first bhūmi are called the Stage of Faith (śraddhā-bhūmi),
while from the first bhūmi upward they are called the Stage of Realization (sākṣātkriyā-bhūmi).
Moreover, in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (Renwang jing):
Those prior to the stages are called "worthy ones" (ārya-pudgala), while those on the stages are called "sages" (ārya).
Alternatively, they may be divided into three categories:
namely, external ordinary beings, internal ordinary beings, and sages.
Those in the stage of the happy destinies are called external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana);
those from the stage of the spiritual lineage (gotra) upward are called internal ordinary beings (adhyātmapṛthagjana);
and those on the stages (bhūmi) are called noble ones (ārya).
Within this, the analysis is conducted through eight sections:
first, the explanation of the names and meanings;
second, the analysis based on the mind of understanding.
The third is distinguished according to the method of understanding;
the fourth is distinguished according to the conditions of understanding;
and the fifth is distinguished according to practice.
Sixth, classification according to afflictions;
seventh, classification according to karma;
eighth, classification according to retribution. First, I shall explain the definitions and meanings [of these categories].
Regarding the term "external ordinary beings" (bāhyapṛthagjana): these are those in the fortunate realms who seek the principle externally;
because they have not yet been able to still mental marks and inwardly take the true nature as their object, they are called "external."
Because the ordinary body of the six realms of transmigration has not yet been cast off,
they are called "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*).

This is like those prior to the stage of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in the Hīnayāna, whose reliance on objects and progression toward contemplation resemble that of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
They are called "outer ordinary beings" (bāhyapṛthagjana). This case is likewise:
they seek the principle by looking outward.
Being identical to the śrāvakas,
they are unable to still mental marks within to seek the ultimate reality;
therefore, they are called "external."
Regarding the term "inner ordinary beings" (ābhyantarapṛthagjana):
because those above the stage of spiritual lineage (gotra) gradually cease [external] conditions and seek the true nature within,
they are called "inner."

Although the segmented stages of the six realms of existence are divided and severed, they have no point of final exhaustion; because the bodies of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are not yet exhausted, they are also called "ordinary.
Therefore, it is said that they are "ordinary" in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*.
As for those called "sages" (ārya), they are those from the first bhūmi upward who have stilled delusion, conformed to the truth, and attained the correct;
thus is the meaning of the term. This concludes the first section.
Next, distinguishing three stages based on the mind of understanding:
there are three kinds of mind. First is the mind of phenomenal consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*).
These are the so-called six consciousnesses and two deluded cognitions,
namely the seventh consciousness.
Third is the true consciousness-mind,
which refers to the eighth consciousness.
During the stage of external ordinary beings, one cultivates contemplative understanding based solely on the phenomenal consciousness (samsaric consciousness).
There is no other meaning.
